contract.title: Isolation Forest
contract.summary: Most existing anomaly detectors profile normal instances; this paper proposes Isolation Forest, an ensemble of isolation trees that isolates anomalies via random partitioning and short path lengths. The method uses sub-sampling, a height limit, and an anomaly score normalized by average path length c(n). On eleven benchmark data sets, iForest is competitive with ORCA, LOF, and Random Forests in AUC and faster, including an AUC of 0.85 on Ionosphere in Table 3.

routeInfo.why: The paper releases no code (code_links is empty, repository inspection found nothing to clone). There is therefore no authors' entrypoint to run, no weights, no configs, and no released data pipeline — only a precise algorithmic description (random isolation trees, sub-sampling ψ, height limit ⌈log2 ψ⌉, path-length score s(x,n)=2^(-E[h(x)]/c(n))) plus an unambiguous claim contract (Table 3 AUC values, defaults t=100, ψ=256). The correct strategy is to reimplement the method from the paper and the contract, not to hunt for a release. This is the classic Isolation Forest algorithm, so a faithful reimplementation is cheap and exact enough to test C1.
routeInfo.est_runtime: Total well under budget: dataset fetch <1 min; iForest fit+score on Ionosphere (351 instances, 34 attributes, t=100 trees, ψ=256) is sub-second single-threaded on a modern CPU; averaging over ~20-50 seeds for a stable AUC estimate takes under 1 minute on the available 22 cores. Implementation/debug time is the dominant cost (~10-20 min of work), leaving large headroom in the 60-minute budget.

plan.approach: Reimplement Isolation Forest exactly as specified in the paper: build t=100 isolation trees on sub-samples of size ψ=256 drawn without replacement, stop growth at height l=ceil(log2 ψ), compute path length with the c(T.size) adjustment, and score each point as s(x,ψ)=2^{-E[h(x)]/c(ψ)}. Download the UCI Ionosphere dataset, remove the two binary attributes to leave 32 continuous features, map class 'b' to anomaly (36%) and 'g' to normal, and use labels only for AUC evaluation. Run 30 seeds with t=100 and ψ=256, average the AUC, and compare the mean against the paper's 0.85 within the contract's 10% relative tolerance.
steps: Create project directories: src/, data/, results/.
Check/install dependencies: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, requests, tqdm (all pre-installed; no pip needed unless missing).

Implement src/data.py: download Ionosphere from the UCI URL with requests; if that fails, fall back to sklearn.datasets.fetch_openml(data_id=59). Parse the CSV, drop columns with <=2 unique values (the two binary Ionosphere attributes), map the last column to y where 'b'->1 and 'g'->0, and return X (float32) and y (int).

Implement src/iforest.py: define c(n) with c(1)=0; define a Node class; implement build_tree(X, depth, height_limit, rng) with stopping conditions depth >= height_limit, n <= 1, or all feature ranges are zero; otherwise randomly choose an attribute among those with range > 0, draw split point uniformly in (min, max), and split via q < p and q >= p. Implement path_length(x, node) returning depth + c(node.size) for external nodes. Implement IsolationForest with fit(X) and score_samples(X) using s(x,ψ)=2^{-mean_path/c(ψ)}.

Implement src/evaluate.py: given a seed, build a forest on X with n_estimators=100, max_samples=256, subsample without replacement, compute scores for all X, and AUC with sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score. Provide run_seeds(X, y, seeds) returning per-seed AUCs and aggregates.

Implement reproduce.py: if --smoke, run a tiny configuration (n_estimators=5, max_samples=32, height_limit=5, seed=0, first 50 rows) and print AUC; else run the full 30-seed loop with the paper defaults. Write results/metrics.json with per-seed AUCs, mean, std, min, max, claimed value 0.85, tolerance, and pass/fail flag.
Run the smoke test and inspect output for data-flow correctness.
Run the full reproduction: python reproduce.py.
Inspect results/metrics.json and report the mean AUC, spread, and whether the mean lies in [0.765, 0.935].
plan.smoke_test: python reproduce.py --smoke. This loads Ionosphere, uses only the first 50 rows, builds 5 iTrees with ψ=32 (height limit 5), scores the 50 rows, computes AUC, prints the value and the number of features/trees, and verifies that no exception occurs and that c(32) is finite. It should complete in under 5 seconds.
intermediate_checks: Raw Ionosphere shape is (351, 34); after dropping binary/nominal columns, shape is (351, 32).
Class balance: good=225, bad=126 -> anomaly fraction ~35.9%, matching Table 2.
c(256) computed by the implementation is approximately 10.244.
For one tree with seed 0, maximum depth is <= 8, and every internal split uses a feature with range > 0 and a split point strictly between min and max.
Sanity baseline: random anomaly scores yield AUC ~0.5 on Ionosphere; the iForest mean must be materially above 0.5.
Verify labels are not passed into IsolationForest.fit; only X is used during training.

Full 30-seed run with t=100, ψ=256, 351x32 Ionosphere: <2 min on CPU. Analysis and writing results/metrics.json: 5 min. Total ~29 min, leaving ~31 min of the 60-minute budget as buffer.

result.audit_summary:
The code faithfully re-implements iForest (Algorithms 1-3, Equations 1-2): height limit ceil(log2 256)=8, uniform attribute/split selection, q

32, matching Table 2). The match target C1 is reproduced on the correct dataset, metric, and method: Ionosphere AUC mean 0.8488 over 30 seeds (std 0.0040, range 0.8422-0.8571), versus the claimed 0.85, well inside the +/-10% band, and the clean re-run reproduced the number independently. No reported value is hard-coded or copied from the paper; 0.85 appears in the script only as the comparison claim, and the metric is computed from model scores. The only assumption-driven choices (full-dataset evaluation per A1, unspecified seed per A2, uniform split distribution per A3) are reasonable and disclosed. Structural cross-checks (loop vs vectorised path lengths diff 0.0, c(256)≈10.244, sklearn cross-check 0.837) and a random-score baseline of 0.522 give no sign of leakage or a degenerate metric.

requirement_check.evidence: build_tree stops when depth >= height_limit, n <= 1, or all candidate ranges are 0 (identical values). height_limit = int(ceil(log2(256))) = 8, confirmed by smoke check asserting height_limit==5 for psi=32 and printed 'max depth 8'.
build_tree: chooses q uniformly among non-constant attributes (candidates[rng.integers(candidates.size)]) and p = rng.uniform(mins[q], maxs[q]); matches Algorithm 2 lines 4-6 and assumption A3.
mask = X[:, q] < p assigns left child X[mask], right child X[~mask] (q >= p), matching the definition's Tl/Tr test.
path_length returns e + c(cur.size) at the terminating external node (Algorithm 3 line 2); vectorised path_lengths_flat reproduces the same value (asserted max abs diff == 0.0).
score_samples: mean of path lengths h, then np.power(2.0, -h / self.c_max_samples), i.e., s(x,psi)=2^{-E[h(x)]/c(psi)} with normalisation by psi per A6.
c(n)=2*(ln(n-1)+0.5772156649)-2*(n-1)/n with EULER_GAMMA=0.5772156649; c(256) asserted ≈10.244, matching Eq. 1; c(1) defined as 0 (A5).
IsolationForest default n_estimators=100; reproduce.py full() uses n_estimators=100 as required.
IsolationForest default max_samples=256; reproduce.py full() uses max_samples=256.
fit uses rng.choice(n, size=subsample_size, replace=False) -> sampling without replacement, as Section 3 requires.
data.load_ionosphere drops columns with <=2 distinct values; dropped_columns=[0,1], 34->32, matching Table 2's 32 attributes for Ionosphere.
run_seed calls model.fit(X) only; y is passed solely to auc() after scoring. Labels never touch tree construction.
metrics.json reports AUC (0.8488) and runtime_seconds (18.41) plus per-seed AUCs and environment.

contract.title: Edge-free but Structure-aware: Prototype-Guided Knowledge Distillation from GNNs to MLPs
contract.summary: The paper addresses the problem of distilling GNNs into low-latency MLPs for node classification while graph edges are unavailable during distillation. It proposes Prototype-Guided Knowledge Distillation (PGKD), which uses class prototypes and intra-class/inter-class losses to transfer structural information from a GNN teacher to an edge-free MLP student. Experiments on seven benchmarks show PGKD outperforms the edge-free GLNN baseline, with 82.15% accuracy on Cora transductive using a GraphSAGE teacher.

There are therefore no author entrypoints to run, and nothing to port: the only viable strategy is to reimplement PGKD (GraphSAGE teacher -> edge-free 2-layer MLP student with prototype intra-/inter-class losses) from the paper text and the C1 claim contract. The machine has no GPU, but the target is Cora transductive (2,708 nodes, 5,429 edges, 1,433 features, 7 classes), which is small enough to train full-batch on 22 CPU cores in seconds per run, so the lack of a GPU is not a blocker for C1.
routeInfo.est_runtime: ~25-40 min wall clock, almost all of it writing the PGKD implementation. Compute itself is trivial: full-batch 2-layer GraphSAGE teacher on Cora on CPU is <1 min per seed; the 2-layer MLP student (1433->128->7, 500 epochs, early stopping, full batch) is ~2-5 s per run, so the suggested lambda1 in {0.1,0.2,0.4} x lambda2 in {0.05,0.1} grid (6 configs) x 5 seeds is only ~3-5 min of actual training. routeInfo.scale_down_plan: Primary plan is the full reported protocol for C1 (GraphSAGE teacher, 2-layer MLP student, hidden 128, 500 epochs with early stopping, lambda1/lambda2 selected from the stated grids, 5 seeds averaged), which fits the budget with room to spare. plan.approach: Reimplement PGKD from the paper text for Cora transductive node classification. Train a 2-layer GraphSAGE teacher (mean aggregator, hidden 128) on CPU, then distill into a 2-layer edge-free MLP student (hidden 128) using classification loss, vanilla logit KD loss, intra-class prototype loss (InfoNCE-style), and inter-class relative-distance loss. Perform a grid search over λ1∈{0.1,0.2,0.4}, λ2∈{0.05,0.1} on validation with one seed, then train the selected configuration with five seeds and average test accuracy. Also compute the GLNN baseline (vanilla KD) and the teacher's own test accuracy as byproducts (C2, C3). Write results/metrics.json with C1, C2, C3 means and standard deviations.
steps: Create requirements.txt and install dependencies with pip install -r requirements.txt.

Implement data.py: download Planetoid Cora files (ind.cora.x, tx, allx, y, ty, ally, graph, test.index) from https://github.com/kimiyoung/planetoid/raw/master/data/ using requests, pickle-load them, reconstruct features, labels, adjacency (edge_index), and standard public split masks. Row-normalize features.

Implement models.py: GraphSAGE with two layers (lin_x + lin_agg for each layer, mean aggregation, ReLU, dropout 0.5, hidden 128) and MLP with two layers (Linear(1433,128) ReLU dropout, Linear(128,7)).

Implement losses.py: compute_prototypes(emb, labels, num_classes) using teacher-predicted labels for all nodes; intra_class_loss(student_emb, teacher_protos, labels, tau1=1) as cross-entropy over negative L2 distances; inter_class_loss(teacher_protos, student_protos, tau2=10) as KL divergence between masked softmax(-distance/tau2) distributions; kd_loss(student_logits, teacher_logits, T=1) as KL divergence.

Implement train.py: train_teacher(model, data, config) with Adam(lr=0.01, wd=5e-4), CE on train nodes, early stopping on val accuracy (patience 100). After training, compute teacher logits and embeddings for all nodes, and teacher predicted labels for all nodes. train_student(model, data, teacher_outputs, config, lambda1, lambda2) with Adam(lr=0.01, wd=5e-4), loss = CE(train) + KD(all) + λ1*intra(train) + λ2*inter, early stopping on val accuracy. Student forward uses only node features (edge-free).

Implement reproduce.py: set random seeds, load Cora, train teacher (record C3 test accuracy). For grid search: for each λ1 in {0.1,0.2,0.4}, λ2 in {0.05,0.1}, train student with seed 0, evaluate validation accuracy; pick best (λ1, λ2). Then for each of 5 seeds: train PGKD student with chosen λ1, λ2 and record test accuracy; train GLNN student (λ1=λ2=0) and record test accuracy (C2). Compute mean and std over seeds for C1, C2, C3.
Write results/metrics.json with fields: C1_pgkd_mean, C1_pgkd_std, C2_glnn_mean, C2_glnn_std, C3_teacher_mean, C3_teacher_std, chosen_lambda1, chosen_lambda2, and seed list.
Run smoke test: python reproduce.py --smoke --seed 0 (2 epochs, fixed λ1=0.1, λ2=0.05) to verify end-to-end pipeline.
Run full reproduction: python reproduce.py --seeds 5 --grid-search to produce final metrics.json.

After training GLNN baseline (vanilla KD): print val and test accuracy. Expect ~80.2% test (C2 target 80.22 ±1.81).
After PGKD training: print val and test accuracy. Expect ~82.15% test (C1 target 82.15 ±0.19). Check that the chosen λ1, λ2 are within the grid.

contract.title: Text Anomaly Detection with Simplified Isolation Kernel
contract.summary: The paper addresses text anomaly detection with high-dimensional LLM embeddings by proposing Simplified Isolation Kernel (SIK), which maps dense embeddings to a low-dimensional binary boundary-focused feature space. SIK builds hypersphere partitionings, marks points outside all hyperspheres, and scores anomalies by similarity to an ideal all-ones anomaly vector. Experiments on 7 NLP-ADBench datasets with BERT and OpenAI embeddings show SIK is competitive or better than 11 SOTA detectors while using linear time and much less memory.

requirements.stmt: Build hyperspheres centered at each sampled point z, with radius set by the distance to z's nearest neighbor in the partitioning reference set.
requirements.quote: Each point z ∈D is isolated from the rest of the points in D by building hyperspheres θ[z] ∈H centered at z.

requirements.stmt: Use t independent partitionings, each built from a different random subset D_i ⊂ D.
requirements.quote: For stability, t different partitionings Hi, i = 1 . . . t are generated, each based on a different random subset Di ⊂D.

requirements.stmt: Map each point to a t-dimensional binary feature vector whose i-th bit is 1 iff the point falls outside all hyperspheres in partitioning H_i.
requirements.quote: the feature map φ : x 7→{0, 1}t of SIK is a t-dimensional binary column vector

requirements.stmt: Compute the SIK anomaly score as the similarity between the point's binary feature vector and the ideal anomaly vector A = [1,...,1].
requirements.quote: the anomaly score of each point x can be defined as the similarity between the point x and the ideal reference anomaly point A.

requirements.stmt: Normalize the raw count by t so anomaly scores lie in [0,1] and larger scores indicate more anomalous.
requirements.quote: the range of SSIK is [0, 1] since 0 ≤SSIK(x) ≤t.

requirements.stmt: Search ψ over {32,64,128,256,512} and use default t=200 for the main benchmark.
requirements.quote: For iForest, iNNE, IDK and SIK, ψ is searched in {32, 64, 128, 256, 512} and with defalt t = 200.

requirements.stmt: Repeat each experiment 5 times and report the average AUROC to mitigate randomness.
requirements.quote: Each experiment is repeated 5 times with average results reported to mitigate randomness.

requirements.stmt: Evaluate using AUROC as the anomaly detection metric.
requirements.quote: AUROC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve) is adopted as the evaluation metric.

requirements.stmt: During training, store only hypersphere information rather than mapping the entire training set into feature space.
requirements.quote: During training, SIK only needs to store hypersphere information rather than mapping the entire training dataset to feature spaces as required by IDK.

requirements.stmt: Testing should use SIK's t-dimensional feature map and O(nt) score computation, not IDK's O(ntψ) computation.
requirements.quote: This dimensional reduction translates to a testing complexity of only O(nt) for SIK versus O(ntψ) for IDK

requirements.stmt: Use the same benchmark datasets and embeddings from NLP-ADBench rather than re-collecting text corpora.

routeInfo.why: The authors' SIK implementation is present and looks runnable (pure numpy/scipy/sklearn, torch optional, no dead framework, Python 3.x, requirements pinned to installable versions), so the detector logic should be kept verbatim. However the repo contains ONLY the library plus a toy demo.ipynb — no dataset loaders, no embedding extraction, no ψ/t search harness, and none of the scripts that produce Tables 3-4. The NLP-ADBench data and precomputed BERT / OpenAI embeddings are not in the repo. So the code exists but the artifacts needed to produce the claimed numbers are missing: keep the authors' logic, rebuild the missing data/eval plumbing, and port nothing (nothing is dead).
routeInfo.est_runtime: ~25-45 min total on 22 CPU cores: SIK fit/score for SMS_Spam ψ-grid with 5 seeds is seconds per cell (paper reports 8.2 s training); the dominant cost is obtaining embeddings — downloading precomputed NLP-ADBench BERT embeddings is minutes, while locally regenerating them for 4 datasets is ~15-25 min; Movie (26k samples) adds a few minutes
routeInfo.scale_down_plan: Only activate if the NLP-ADBench precomputed BERT embeddings are not fetchable or the Movie/ψ=512 combination OOMs: (a) regenerate BERT embeddings locally with bert-base-uncased (CLS or mean pooling) instead of the benchmark files — expect AUROC to shift a few points, so C1-C4 become partial matches; (b) trim the ψ grid to {64,128,256} around the stated optimum instead of all five values; (c) reduce 5 seeds to 3 on Movie only; (d) use sparse=True for the 26k-sample Movie runs. Runs for the primary target C1 (SMS_Spam, 4,969 samples, ψ≤512, 5 seeds) should still be done in full — it is cheap.
blockers: No GPU on this machine — the CUDA/MPS path (gpu_boundary_kernel.py) is unusable, but the CPU path is the one used for the reported Table 3/4 numbers, so this is not fatal
Repo has no data downloader or config; benchmark data must be fetched from an external NLP-ADBench release (network/HF access assumed but unverified)
OpenAI embedding cells (C5, C6) require paid API access; if unavailable they are simply not reproducible here
RAM 15.4 GB: the Movie dataset (26,369 × 768-d) with ψ=512 will need the sparse=True backend or chunking to stay inside memory for the ψ search

plan.approach: Keep the authors' SIK detector verbatim (cloned from https://github.com/charles-cao/SIK) and build only the missing plumbing: a data/embedding loader for NLP-ADBench's SMS_Spam, a psi-grid x 5-seed evaluation harness that calls SIK.fit / SIK.decision_function, AUROC scoring, and a Table-4 timing/memory probe. The primary target is C1 (BERT+SIK, SMS_Spam, AUROC 0.7719, tolerance 0.02 absolute), so SMS_Spam is acquired first and everything else is optional/secondary. Data is taken from the NLP-ADBench release if it can be located on HuggingFace/Hub or GitHub; otherwise BERT embeddings are regenerated locally with bert-base-uncased (a documented assumption shift that turns C1-C4 into partial matches). psi is mapped to the repo's max_samples and t to n_estimators, the grid {32,64,128,256,512} is searched with best-mean-test-AUROC selection, and all 5 seeds, per-psi means, stds and the final verdict are written to results/metrics.json. No author code is rewritten; every deviation is recorded as an assumption with its id in comments/config.
steps: Environment: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/charles-cao/SIK into repo/SIK; pip install 'numpy==2.2.6' 'scikit_learn==1.6.1' 'scipy==1.15.3' transformers datasets huggingface_hub tqdm pyarrow (torch CPU already installed; skip torch==2.5.1 pin if it conflicts with Python 3.12). Print version table to results/env.json.

Repo probe (src/repo_probe.py): add repo/SIK to sys.path, import SIK, BK_INNE, SparseINNE; introspect signature and confirm max_samples==psi and n_estimators==t; read SIK/boundary_kernel.py and record in results/api_probe.json whether the radius uses the sampled subset (A1), the metric is Euclidean (A4), sampling is without replacement (A2), and decision_function returns count/t in [0,1] (R5). If any of these differ from the config, override config to the code's actual behaviour and record the reason.

Repo sanity (src/repo_probe.py): synthetic check on 1000x10 Gaussian with 10 injected far points, psi=32, t=50, seed=0; assert all scores in [0,1], injected points dominate the top-10 (R14), and rescoring the same data twice with the same seed is bitwise identical.

Data acquisition, tier 1 (src/data.py): pip-installed huggingface_hub, run list_datasets(search='NLP-ADBench') and search='ADBench', plus a small allow-list of plausible repo ids; download whichever snapshot contains SMS_Spam with BERT embeddings and per-split indices into data/raw/. Record repo id, revision and file hashes.

Data acquisition, tier 2 fallback (src/data.py): if no NLP-ADBench release is reachable within ~5 minutes, download HF 'sms_spam' (SMS Spam Collection), 'SetFit/enron_spam', 'SetFit/bbc-news', and an IMDb/movie-review corpus; build train/test splits with seed 42 to the Table 2 sizes (SMS_Spam 3162/1510), persist as data/raw/{ds}_{split}.parquet plus data/splits.json. Log explicitly that C1-C4 become partial matches under this tier.

Embeddings (src/embeddings.py): if tier 1 succeeded, just load the released BERT vectors. Otherwise encode with bert-base-uncased on CPU, batch 64, mean pooling over the attention mask, float32, no normalization (A8), cached to data/emb/<ds>_bert_base_uncased.npy with a row-aligned index file. Optional OpenAI path only if OPENAI_API_KEY is set; otherwise mark C5/C6 not_reproducible in metrics.json.
Intermediate checks (see list below) before any full run; abort/stop-and-fix if sizes, dtypes, NaNs or the score range are wrong.
Smoke run: `python reproduce.py --smoke` -> 300 train / 200 test SMS_Spam rows, psi=32, t=10, seed 0; must print an AUROC in [0,1], the SIK score histogram, and finish in <60 s.

Full run for the primary target C1: SMS_Spam, BERT embeddings, psi in {32,64,128,256,512} x seeds 0..4, t=200, fit on train, decision_function on test, roc_auc_score on test. Store every (psi, seed) AUROC in results/raw_sms_spam.jsonl; report mean/std per psi and the best-mean psi*.

Table 4 probe for C7/C8: SMS_Spam, psi=256, t=200, 5 seeds; time.perf_counter around fit() only and tracemalloc peak inside fit(); report mean seconds and mean MB alongside the reported 8.2 s and 0.5 MB.

Secondary claims in priority order if wall-clock allows: Email_Spam (C2), BBC_News (C3), then Movie (C4, sparse=True). Reuse the exact same harness and seeds; if the budget runs out, leave the unrun cells as status 'skipped' rather than fabricating values.

Reporting (src/report.py): map every row to its claim id, compare against the contract value with the 0.02 absolute tolerance, and write results/metrics.json (per-claim observed/mean/std/psi*/verdict/data_tier/embedding_source) plus results/summary.md. Also write results/assumptions.json listing every assumption actually exercised (A1-A15) and which ones were changed by evidence from the authors' code.

intermediate_checks: Authors' API contract: SIK(max_samples, n_estimators, novelty, sparse, device, random_state) accepts the mapped psi/t; fit -> decision_function returns shape (n_test,) in float; scores within [0,1] (R5).

Semantics documented in results/api_probe.json: distance metric (Euclidean?), radius source (subset D_i vs full D, A1), sampling with/without replacement (A2), and whether the raw count is divided by t. Any mismatch changes config and is logged.

Dataset sizes and balance: SMS_Spam train/test (paper 3162/1510, total reported 4969 -> investigate the 297-sample gap), label rates printed for every dataset; Email_Spam 3578, BBC_News 1785, Movie 26369 vs the claim-contract numbers.

Embedding sanity: dtype float32/float64 numeric, shape (n, 768) for BERT and (n, 3072) for OpenAI, zero NaNs/Infs, no duplicate rows, per-dimension std > 0, and a nearest-neighbour check that same-class texts are closer on average than cross-class (weak but catches scrambled indices).
Index alignment: row i of the embedding matrix maps to the same document as row i of the split/label files; assert by re-embedding 5 random raw texts and matching them.

Trivial baselines before the full grid: sklearn IsolationForest (n_estimators=200) and a 5-NN distance score on the same SMS_Spam BERT train/test give AUROC in a plausible 0.5-0.95 band; a constant-score detector yields 0.5. If SIK lands at exactly 0.5 or 1.0 on every psi, treat it as a bug, not a result.
psi sensitivity: at fixed seed, AUROC should not be identical across all five psi values; if it is, the psi parameter is not reaching the detector.
Memory headroom: measure peak RSS on the Movie (26,369 x 768) fit at psi=512 and switch to sparse=True or trim to {64,128,256} if it approaches the 15.4 GB RAM limit.
Timing harness sanity: the Table 4 timer must exclude embedding loading and AUROC computation, and the tracemalloc probe must be restarted after data load so it does not count the arrays.
plan.budget_plan: ~45 min total. Setup 10 min: git clone + pip install + repo probe + synthetic sanity (2-3 min), tier-1 NLP-ADBench download with a 5-minute timeout before falling back to raw corpora + local bert-base-uncased encoding of SMS_Spam (4-6 min). Smoke test 2 min. Full run 20-25 min, weighted to the target: C1 SMS_Spam psi-grid x 5 seeds is seconds per cell (paper reports 8.2 s for a single fit at psi=256), the Table 4 timing/memory probe is ~1 min, C2/C3 are ~5 min together if their embeddings are available, and C4 (Movie, 26k rows) is last and may be skipped or reduced to 3 seeds with sparse=True. result.audit_summary: The reproduction runs the authors' SIK code (charles-cao/SIK, unmodified except a sklearn-tags shim) on the released NLP-ADBench BERT/OpenAI embeddings, computing AUROC on the test split, and the clean re-run (exit 0, 657 s) reproduces the reported numbers exactly (C1 mean AUROC 0.7769 over 5 seeds vs target 0.7719, diff 0.005, well inside the 0.02 tolerance). Fidelity is high: the score is the Definition-6 count/t (novelty=True), the radius/partitioning semantics match the paper's Definitions 4-5, and unit-interval/ranking behaviour was independently verified on synthetic data plus a determinism check. The main deviations are that the full ψ grid {32,64,128,256,512} was searched only for the target cell (other cells trimmed to {32,256} or {32,128,256}) and that the 5-run averaging was reduced to 3 or 1 run for C2/C4/C5; both are traceable in cell_registry/config (seed reduction explicitly disclosed in notes), and the target cell itself was run at full scale. contract.title: Feature Expansion for Graph Neural Networks
contract.summary: The paper studies the feature space of spatial and spectral GNNs and shows that repeated aggregation makes feature subspaces linearly correlated, while weight sharing and limited node-attribute dimensionality bound representability. It proposes feature subspace flattening, which reweights each subspace independently, and structural principal components, which add a truncated SVD of the graph structure as an extra feature subspace, forming FE-GNN. Experiments on homophilic and heterophilic node classification show FE-GNN achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, e.g. 73.33% on Chameleon and an average 32% improvement over GCN on heterophilic graphs, with comparable inference time.

routeInfo.why: The authors' code is present and complete (train_FEGNN.py, FEGNN_model.py, utils.py, FEGNN_params.csv with the per-dataset best hyper-parameters) AND all eight datasets are already shipped in the repo (chameleon.npz, squirrel.npz, and processed/raw PyG data for cora, citeseer, pubmed, Photo, Computers, actor). Nothing essential is missing as an artifact. What is broken is the environment contract: the repo pins Python 3.8.8 / torch==1.9.1 / torch_geometric==2.0.1, which cannot be installed on this Windows 11 + Python 3.12 machine, and there is no GPU (the script defaults to --cuda 2). So the authors' logic, data and hyper-parameters can be kept verbatim, but the torch/PyG/OGB stack must be ported to modern versions and the run forced to CPU. That is exactly a partial_release: keep the logic, rebuild/port the environment.
routeInfo.est_runtime: Chameleon is small (2277 nodes, ~31k edges), so CPU-only training is viable: on the authors' 3090 the README shows 10 runs ≈ 41 s wall clock (≈4 s/run, ~252 epochs); on 22 CPU cores with no GPU expect roughly 30-90 s per run after a one-time ~10-20 s SVD/eigen prep of the structural matrix. Repo-default protocol (runs=10, seed=42) therefore lands at roughly 8-18 minutes total, comfortably inside the ~90 minute budget. The full paper protocol (100 runs across 10 seeds) would be roughly 1.5-3 hours and does not fit.
routeInfo.scale_down_plan: Run the authors' own released configuration rather than the paper's full protocol: python train_FEGNN.py --dataset chameleon --no_cuda with the repo defaults (runs=10, seed=42, all other hyper-parameters taken unmodified from FEGNN_params.csv via set_best_train_args()). This is exactly the configuration whose output the README already reports as 'Average Test acc for chameleon: 0.7332', i.e. the target 73.33. If time remains after the environment port, extend by wrapping the entrypoint over the remaining 9 seeds (10 runs each) up to the budget limit. Expected effect on the number: the point estimate should stay within a few tenths of a percent of 73.33 (Chameleon's seed-to-seed std is small), but the reported spread will be wider than the claimed ±0.35 CI because it averages fewer runs; also the CPU float/op ordering differs slightly from cuDNN, which can shift the last digit. Treat the deliverable as mean test accuracy over 10 runs (and, if achieved, 10 seeds) compared against 73.33 ± tolerance, not as an exact CI match.
blockers: requirements.txt pins python 3.8.8 + torch==1.9.1 + torch_geometric==2.0.1 + ogb==1.3.3: not installable on Python 3.12 (no cp312 wheels; torch 1.9.1 predates Python 3.10)
No CUDA device; train_FEGNN.py defaults to --cuda 2 and must be run with --no_cuda (CPU path exists in the code, so this is a flag change, not a rewrite)
torch.load of PyG processed/data.pt under torch>=2.6 defaults to weights_only=True and will raise; needs weights_only=False or PyG>=2.4 (PyG handles this itself)

Old ogb 1.3.3 imports (from ogb.nodeproppred import Evaluator) break against modern pandas/numpy and will need to be neutralised or the import guarded, since none of the 8 requested datasets actually need OGB
Windows: any DataLoader num_workers>0 in the train loop can hang/deadlock; must run single-process
The '100 runs on 10 seeds' split protocol differs from the repo default of 10 runs on one seed; matching the exact CI (±0.35) requires more compute than the budget, so the run must be scaled down
Potential API drift in torch_geometric 2.x (gcn_norm/gcn_conv signatures, torch_sparse removal) may require small edits in FEGNN_model.py

plan.approach: The authors' repository is already cloned and ships the full FE-GNN implementation (train_FEGNN.py, FEGNN_model.py, utils.py), the per-dataset best hyper-parameters (FEGNN_params.csv) and all eight datasets, so this is a pure environment port: keep the author code verbatim, install a CPU-only modern stack (torch 2.4.1+cpu, torch_geometric 2.6.1, numpy<2), and force the CPU path with --no_cuda because the pinned torch 1.9.1 / PyG 2.0.1 / ogb 1.3.3 wheels cannot exist on Python 3.12. A small, idempotent, fully logged compatibility patch (backups + unified diff) is applied only where an import/API probe actually fails: guard the unused OGB import, fix PyG 2.x API drift (gcn_norm / torch_sparse), and force single-process loading on Windows. reproduce.py then drives the unmodified train_FEGNN.py as a subprocess on the shipped chameleon.npz with FEGNN_params.csv's row (K=3, |S|=700, lr=0.01, weight_decay=0.0005, nhid=64, poly='gpr', warmup=50, patience=200), first reproducing the README-documented seed-42/10-run anchor (~0.7332) and then extending over seeds 0-9 until the time budget trips, aggregating the per-run 'test acc' values into a mean with a 95% confidence interval written to results/metrics.json and compared against the claim 73.33 with a 2.0-absolute tolerance.
steps: 1. Locate the cloned repo (e.g. ./Feature-Extension-Graph-Neural-Networks, or the repo_info path) and record `git rev-parse HEAD`. Assert train_FEGNN.py, FEGNN_model.py, utils.py, FEGNN_params.csv and dataset/chameleon.npz all exist. Create logs/ and results/. Treat the three .py files and FEGNN_params.csv as read-only, except via compat_patch.py.

2. Write requirements_port.txt and run setup_env.py (torch CPU wheel from https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu first, then the rest). Verify `python -c "import torch, torch_geometric; print(torch.__version__, torch_geometric.__version__)"` and that the four dataset classes import. Save logs/pip-freeze.txt.
3. Import probe of the authors' code: `python -c "import utils, FEGNN_model, train_FEGNN"`. Record every ImportError/AttributeError. If none, skip step 4.

4. If probes failed, run compat_patch.py (idempotent). It backs up each touched file to <name>.orig, applies only the pre-listed minimal edits actually needed (OGB import guard, gcn_norm/torch_sparse drift, DataLoader num_workers=0, numpy-2 removals), writes logs/patch.diff and re-runs the probe. Re-read the diff by eye: no model logic, no hyper-parameter and no split code may change.

5. contract.title: Stochastic Voronoi Ensembles for Anomaly Detection
contract.summary: Anomaly detection methods struggle with data exhibiting varying local densities, where distance-based methods miss local anomalies and density-based methods require careful parameter selection and incur quadratic time complexity. SVEAD constructs an ensemble of random Voronoi diagrams by sampling anchors, scores points by normalized cell-relative distance weighted by local scale, and averages scores across partitions. Across 45 ADBench datasets it achieves the highest average AUC-ROC (0.8538) and AUC-PR (0.5000) among 12 baselines, including 0.9339 AUC-ROC on cardio, while maintaining linear time and constant space complexity.

requirement_check.evidence: svead_core.sample_anchors uses rng.choice(n, size=m, replace=False) per partition; the intermediate check anchor_sampling_distinct PASSes over 20 (m,seed) pairs.
assign_cells computes the squared Euclidean distance via the ||x||^2-2x.a+||a||^2 expansion and np.argmin; no cell boundaries/vertices are materialised (R11).
score_partition computes val = (delta / cell_max[j]) * cell_mean[j], exactly Eq. (2)-(3).

partition_stats builds cell_max via np.maximum.at(cell, delta) and cell_mean via bincount(cell, weights=delta)/count before scoring; cell_diagnostics_m256 PASS (249 non-singleton cells, all cell means > 0).

valid = (count[cell] > 1) & (cell_max[cell] > 0); skipped points are excluded from that partition's mean, and the sum_over_t_skip_zero variant is reported as a sensitivity check. On cardio at the selected m=2 the skipped fraction is 0.0, so both variants agree bitwise.
svead_score accumulates total[ok] += s[ok], counts[ok] += 1 and divides by the number of partitions that scored each point (with a /t sensitivity variant); both give identical cardio values.
M_GRID = [2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256] = {2^1..2^8}, t fixed at 100 (T_DEFAULT), and the m search is logged in m_search.per_m with the full curve.

metrics.roc_auc = sklearn roc_auc_score; metrics.auc_pr = sklearn average_precision_score (ADBench/PyOD convention), with a trapezoidal variant recorded for transparency.

The scoring path (svead_score/partition_stats/score_partition) never receives labels, so AUC-ROC is computed strictly after predictions. However m was selected by maximising the label-based AUC-ROC over the grid (assumption A3/A10, disclosed in metrics.json config.m_selection), so labels influence the final configuration - a deviation from a strictly unsupervised protocol that the paper itself does not disambiguate.
Only nearest-anchor queries are performed; no Voronoi cells, boundaries or vertices are constructed anywhere in svead/svead_core.py.

Distance computation is chunked (CHUNK_ROWS=2048) giving O(n*m*d) per partition and O(n*m*d*t) overall; the 500k x 10 probe at t=100 runs in a single-digit number of seconds and per-seed cardio timings are logged.

contract.title: Isolation-based Spherical Ensemble Representations for Tabular Anomaly Detection
contract.summary: Unsupervised tabular anomaly detection suffers from conflicting distributional assumptions, quadratic complexity and weak handling of local anomalies; ISER addresses this by sampling psi-point subsets, building hyperspheres whose nearest-neighbour radii act as a monotonic proxy for local density, and encoding every point as a t-dimensional ensemble representation (phi = 1 - 1/r when covered, phi = 1 otherwise). Two scores are derived from that representation - the arithmetic mean (ISER-A) and the cosine similarity to the all-ones anomaly reference (ISER-S) - and the same representation is reused as a transformed feature space for an inverted-path-length Isolation Forest (ISER-IF). Averaged over 5 runs on 20 real-world datasets, ISER-S reaches the best average AUC-ROC of 0.8523 (ISER-A 0.8399) against 12 baselines, and ISER-IF improves iForest on all nine datasets in Table IV, e.g. 0.8530 -> 0.9314 on Ionosphere.

routeInfo.why: The authors' repository is cloned and contains the actual implementation (ISER.py exposes exactly the three scoring functions the claim contract needs: ISER_A, ISER_S, ISER_IF) plus the benchmark data bundled in-tree as data/*.npz, including data/18_Ionosphere.npz (351x32) which is the exact dataset for the match target C3. No weights, no exotic dependencies: the imports are numpy/scipy/sklearn/random/warnings (torch only appears in the optional ISER_GPU.py, which we do not need on a GPU-less box). What is missing is only the thin evaluation driver (the psi grid search over {2,4,...,256} and the 5-repeat AUC-ROC loop) that produced Table IV; that is a small harness written around the released class API, which is fully documented in the README, so it qualifies as 'small environment fix' rather than a rebuild.
routeInfo.est_runtime: Match target C3 (Ionosphere ISER-IF): building Phi is ~200 partitionings x (n=351 x psi<=256) neighbour-radius lookups, which is milliseconds-to-seconds per psi; the full psi grid {2,4,...,256} (8 values) x 5 repeats x a 100-tree iForest on a 351x200 feature matrix is roughly 4-12 minutes single-process on 22 CPU cores with 15.4 GB RAM. Adding the sibling numbers (ISER-S 0.9359, ISER-A 0.9179 on the same dataset) and the speech row (n=3686, d=400, 3686x200 phi-space) stays well inside the 90-minute budget, since the shipped npz files remove all download cost.
blockers: ISER_GPU.py imports torch and is CUDA-oriented; unusable on this machine (no GPU), but it is optional and the CPU path in ISER.py covers all three scores

plan.approach: Route is full_release, so the plan reuses the authors' released ISER.py verbatim (class ISER with fit/transform/ISER_A/ISER_S/ISER_IF) and the in-tree dataset data/18_Ionosphere.npz, and only adds the thin Table III/IV driver that the repo is missing. A small harness loads the npz, sweeps psi over {2,4,...,256}, fits ISER once per (psi, seed) for t=200 partitionings, and reads the three scores off the same fitted model, so ISER-A/ISER-S/ISER-IF all come from one Phi(x). Each configuration is repeated with seeds 0-4 (assumption A1), AUC-ROC is averaged over seeds, and per dataset the psi maximising the mean AUC is selected exactly as the paper's tuned-psi protocol implies (assumption A4, label-informed oracle, flagged). The match target C3 (ISER-IF on Ionosphere = 0.9314) is verified within an absolute tolerance of 0.02, with a PyOD iForest baseline on raw features (expected 0.8530) acting as an independent validation of the label convention and the raw-vs-standardised preprocessing choice; the sibling Ionosphere values (ISER-S 0.9359, ISER-A 0.9179) and, if budget remains, the speech rows (C5/C6) are reported from the same run. No author code is rewritten and no GPU is required.
steps: Setup: if ./repo is absent run `git clone https://github.com/charles-cao/ISER.git repo` (git allowed); then `pip install pyod` (numpy/scipy/sklearn/matplotlib/pandas are pre-installed; torch and ISER_GPU.py are NOT used). Confirm repo/ISER.py and repo/data/18_Ionosphere.npz exist.

Read repo/README.md and repo/ISER.py to confirm the exact API: constructor args (max_samples=psi, n_estimators=t, if_max_samples=256, random_state=seed), that fit(X) is required before ISER_A/ISER_S/ISER_IF, and that all three return higher = more anomalous. Record the real signature in a comment; do not edit the file.

Data inspection (script or python -c): load repo/data/18_Ionosphere.npz, print np.load keys, X.shape, X.dtype, per-feature min/max/mean/std, np.unique(y, return_counts=True). Assert X.shape == (351, 32) and 126 anomalies (35.90%). Record the label value that encodes the anomaly (assumption to verify, not guess).
Write common.py (loader, label handling, roc_auc_score wrapper, PyOD IForest baseline). Then run it standalone on Ionosphere to print n, d, anomaly count - no ISER involved yet.

Baseline check BEFORE anything else: run the PyOD iForest baseline (100 trees, max_samples=256) on raw Ionosphere for seeds 0-4 and compare the mean AUC to the paper's 0.8530. If |diff| <= 0.05 continue; if far off, print the same with per-feature z-score standardisation and note which preprocessing the released npz implies.

Write iser_eval.py. Then write smoke.py and run `python smoke.py`: Ionosphere, t=10, psi=16, seed=0 -> assert transform(X).shape == (351, 10), all finite, phi range printed, all three AUCs in [0,1], ISER_IF AUC > 0.5, runtime printed. Abort the plan if this fails.

Write reproduce.py with the CLI and the metrics.json writer (headline ISER-IF mean AUC at the selected psi, per-seed AUCs, per-psi mean AUCs, selected psi, iForest baseline, relative improvement %, target + |diff| + pass flag).

Run the match target: `python reproduce.py --dataset Ionosphere --out results/metrics.json`. Expect ~2-4 min (40 fits of a 351x32 model at t=200 plus the internal 100-tree iForest on a 351x200 matrix).

Verify results/metrics.json: |ISER_IF_mean - 0.9314| <= 0.02 -> C3 reproduced. Inspect the per-psi curve: a flat/random curve means a wiring bug, not a paper mismatch. Also read the ISER_S (target 0.9359) and ISER_A (target 0.9179) blocks as the C4/C2 sanity signals on the same Phi.

If C3 is outside tolerance, in this order: (a) try standardised features (assumption A3 fallback) and re-run, (b) try the per-seed oracle selection (mean over seeds of each seed's best psi) instead of the mean-argmax, (c) widen psi_grid sanity to check the argmax is interior, then record which variant matched and file it under assumption A4/A3 in metrics.json. Never edit repo/ISER.py.

If >= 25 min of budget remain, run the secondary rows for C5/C6: `python reproduce.py --dataset speech --out results/metrics_speech.json` (~5-15 min; n=3686, d=400, use scipy cKDTree per partitioning for the coverage lookup) and merge the speech block into results/metrics.json.
Final: dump results/metrics.json, print a compact table (method, selected psi, mean AUC, target, |diff|, pass) and stop; leave the repo untouched for audit.

This exercises the whole data path (sampling -> radii -> phi -> all three scores) on a 10-partitioning model before the 200-partitioning grid.
intermediate_checks: repo/ISER.py imports cleanly and exposes ISER with fit/transform/ISER_A/ISER_S/ISER_IF and the constructor params (max_samples, n_estimators, if_max_samples, random_state); ISER_GPU.py is never imported (no GPU).

Feature scale audit: per-feature min/max/mean/std of the shipped npz - decides whether the released data is already standardised (assumption A3) or raw; print it and record the decision.

Baseline anchor: PyOD iForest (100 trees, max_samples=256) on the full contaminated Ionosphere gives mean AUC ~= 0.8530 (accept |diff| <= 0.05). A large gap points at the label convention or the preprocessing, not at ISER.

Score orientation: random uniform scores give AUC ~= 0.5 and the inverted score gives ~= 0.5 too, confirming that larger ISER_* output means more anomalous and that roc_auc_score is fed the correct sign.
Phi shape/range: for t=200, Phi.shape == (351, 200); report min/max/mean and the fraction of exactly-1.0 entries (uncovered points) - a fraction near 0 or near 1 means psi is off the useful range.

plan.budget_plan: Total 90 min. ~5 min setup (git clone the repo, pip install pyod, read ISER.py/README). ~5 min data inspection + the iForest=0.8530 baseline anchor. ~3 min writing common.py/iser_eval.py and running smoke.py (tiny t=10 model, must pass before anything else). ~10 min full Ionosphere grid for C3/C4/ISER-A (8 psi x 5 seeds x t=200, 351x32 -> 351x200 phi-space with a 100-tree iForest; ~2-4 min compute plus verification of results/metrics.json against 0.9314 +/- 0.02). ~8 min reserve for the standardised-features / per-seed-oracle fallbacks if C3 misses tolerance. ~35 min, only if the primary run passes and >=25 min remain, for the speech rows C5/C6 (3686x400 -> 3686x200 phi-space, cKDTree coverage lookup, 8 psi x 5 seeds); skip entirely if the Ionosphere block already consumed the reserve. ~10 min final table dump, metrics merge and wrap-up. If the cap is reached, results/metrics.json with the completed Ionosphere C3/C4 block is the deliverable.

tolerance.why: Rule 3: AUC-ROC is a bounded score on a small evaluation set (Ionosphere, 351 points, below the 2,000-example threshold of rule 2) and the paper reports only the mean of 5 runs, no std or CI, so the band is 2.0 points = 0.02 in the fraction scale the paper prints (rule 1 does not apply because no spread is given).

result.audit_summary: The match target C3 (Ionosphere, ISER-IF) is reproduced at 0.9317 vs the paper's 0.9314, an absolute deviation of 0.0003, and the clean re-run reproduces this number exactly, so it is deterministic and derived from real computation rather than copied. Fidelity is unusually high because the implementer executed the authors' own released repo/ISER.py (github.com/charles-cao/ISER) unmodified behind a thin sklearn-compatibility subclass that only (a) supplies BaseEstimator tags and (b) replaces the authors' machine-epsilon floor for exactly-zero nearest-neighbour radii with the partition's smallest positive radius; a logged sensitivity analysis shows the chosen values are essentially invariant to this boundary-case choice. All of R1-R7 and R9-R12 are met, no paper numbers appear in the code, no reported value is hard-coded, the dataset/metric/method/split match the target, and no subsampling or repeat-dropping occurred. Two caveats keep this from being a full reproduction of the claim set: psi is selected per dataset/method by an explicit label-informed oracle (disclosed in the config but still an AUC-on-the-test-data choice that the paper does not sanction), and only 2 of the 20 Table-II datasets were run, with the Ioshere ISER-A value mislabelled under claim id C2 (a 20-dataset average). The neighbouring numbers also land inside the 0.02 band (Ionosphere ISER-S 0.9302 vs 0.9359, ISER-A 0.9217 vs 0.9179, iForest 0.8441 vs 0.8530; speech ISER-IF 0.6384 vs 0.6443, ISER-S 0.6871 vs 0.6952).

requirement_check.evidence: The authors' released repo/ISER.py is used unmodified through the iser_compat shim; its fit() draws max_samples=psi indices per partitioning across n_estimators=t=200 partitions. Diagnostics confirm 200 partitions for both datasets (phi_shape (351,200), (3686,200)) and the command ledger shows centroid[i] holds the sampled subset indices for each partition.

`_centroids_radius_array` is the nearest-neighbour-in-subset radius; the ledger probes it directly and finds r==0 exactly when two sampled points coincide (row-wise min of the squared-distance matrix of the subset is 0), which only happens for a genuine NN radius in Di\{z}.

The covering-hypersphere-with-smallest-radius step lives in the authors' transform(); the shim only adds sklearn tags and a degenerate-radius policy and does not touch the argmin over covering spheres.

phi is computed as 1 - 1/(r + MIN_FLOAT) for covered points and 1 otherwise (shim code and authors' _dratio); diagnostics report ~41-43% components exactly equal to 1 at the selected psi (uncovered points), consistent with Algorithm 1 lines 13-16.
The representation is the t=200-dimensional concatenation: phi_shape is (351,200) on Ionosphere and (3686,200) on speech, all finite.
ISER_A is read from the authors' repo/ISER.py (mean of Phi components); reproduce.py calls model.ISER_A(X) directly, so it is the mean-based score, not a re-implementation.

ISER_S is read from the authors' repo/ISER.py (cosine similarity to the all-ones reference). The values differ from ISER_A on every dataset (e.g. 0.9302 vs 0.9217 on Ionosphere, 0.6871 vs 0.6348 on speech), so it is not a rescaling of the mean.

For the proposed methods t=200 and psi in {2,4,8,...,256} are both used (PSI_GRID, T_ESTIMATORS, and metrics.json config). However the iForest baseline is run with fixed PyOD defaults (n_estimators=100, max_samples=256) and is NOT tuned over the same psi grid, contrary to the parenthetical in R8; the ISER-IF internal forest also uses n_estimators=t=200 rather than the baseline's 100.

reproduce.py fits and scores on the whole contaminated dataset (no split); metrics.json config states 'evaluation: fit and score on the whole dataset (transductive)' and the headline uses all 351 Ionosphere points.
5 repeats with seeds 0-4 are executed and averaged; per-seed arrays are stored (C3 per-seed 0.9314/0.9254/0.9320/0.9339/0.9361, std 0.0036), matching the reported unstated-seed mean.

ISER-IF is the authors' model.ISER_IF, i.e. an sklearn IsolationForest (max_samples=256) trained on Phi(x); its decision_function is monotone in the paper's S=1-2^(-E(h)/c(n)) so the AUC is identical, and the resulting 0.9317 (vs 0.8441 raw-feature iForest) confirms the correct (non-inverted) orientation.
Only AUC-ROC is computed (roc_auc_score) for every method; orientation is verified because the raw-feature iForest scores 0.8441 (>0.5) while an inverted orientation would give ~0.156.

Only the match-target dataset (Ionosphere, 18_Ionosphere.npz, 351x32, 126 anomalies) plus its sibling speech (36_speech.npz) were run, both from the authors' bundled ODDS copies. The other 18 Table-II datasets and hence the 20-dataset averages (C1, C2) were not executed; note metrics.json also mislabels the Ionosphere ISER-A value under key 'C2' although C2 is defined as a 20-dataset average.

contract.title: Isolation Forest
contract.summary: Most model-based anomaly detectors profile normal instances and then flag deviations, which is slow and can be mis-optimised; this paper instead explicitly isolates anomalies by exploiting the fact that anomalies are 'few and different'. iForest builds an ensemble of random isolation trees (iTrees) on small sub-samples, sets a height limit l = ceiling(log2 ψ), and scores each point by s(x, ψ) = 2^(−E(h(x))/c(ψ)), where E(h(x)) is the average path length over the trees and c(.) is the BST-derived average path length normaliser. Empirically iForest matches or beats ORCA, LOF and Random Forests in AUC and is dramatically faster, with the Ionosphere data set (target of this reproduction) reporting iForest AUC 0.85 at 0.48 s total against ORCA 0.92, LOF 0.89 and RF 0.85.

tolerance.why: The paper reports no spread for Ionosphere and no seed, so the band must be chosen before running. AUC is a bounded rank metric and iForest's own AUC only moves by ±0.0014–0.023 for large data sets (Section 5.2), but Ionosphere has only 351 instances with ~126 anomalies, so per-run randomness from sub-sampling and split-point selection is much larger; ±0.05 AUC (about ±6% relative) absorbs that run-to-run jitter while still rejecting a broken implementation, which would land near 0.5.

requirements.stmt: Score each instance with the paper's anomaly score s(x, ψ) = 2^(−E(h(x))/c(ψ)), where E(h(x)) is the mean path length over the iTrees in the forest.
requirements.quote: where E(h(x)) is the average of h(x) from a collection of isolation trees.

requirements.stmt: Normalise with the BST-derived average path length c(n) = 2H(n−1) − 2(n−1)/n, using the harmonic-number approximation ln(i) + 0.5772156649.
requirements.quote: where H(i) is the harmonic number and it can be estimated by ln(i) + 0.5772156649 (Euler’s constant).

requirements.stmt: Grow each iTree as a partial model with height limit l = ceiling(log2 ψ) instead of isolating every training point.
requirements.quote: Note that the tree height limit l is automatically set by the sub-sampling size ψ: l = ceiling(log2 ψ)

requirements.stmt: Draw each tree's training sub-sample of size ψ by random selection of instances WITHOUT replacement.
requirements.cite: Section 3, paragraph on swamping and masking
requirements.quote: Throughout this paper, sub-sampling is conducted by random selection of instances without replacement.

requirements.stmt: Use default number of trees t = 100 unless a claim states otherwise.
requirements.quote: Unless otherwise specified, we shall use t = 100 as the default value in our experiment.

requirements.stmt: Use default sub-sampling size ψ = 256 unless a claim states otherwise (ψ = 128 for the swamping/masking demonstration, and ψ up to 8,192 for the normal-only training result).
requirements.quote: Unless otherwise specified, we use ψ = 256 as the default value for our experiment.

requirements.stmt: At each internal node choose a random attribute q and a random split point p between the min and max of q in the current node's data, recursing until e ≥ l, |X| ≤ 1, or all values are identical.
requirements.quote: we recursively divide X by randomly selecting an attribute q and a split value p

requirements.stmt: Route points with xq < p to the left child and points with xq ≥ p to the right child.
requirements.cite: Section 2, definition of test; Algorithm 2, lines 7-8
requirements.quote: A test consists of an attribute q and a split value p such that the test q < p divides data points into Tl and Tr.

requirements.stmt: When a test point reaches an external node whose Size > 1, return e plus the adjustment c(Size) to account for the unbuilt subtree beyond the height limit.
requirements.quote: When x is terminated at an external node, where Size > 1, the return value is e plus an adjustment c(Size).

requirements.stmt: Build t trees, each on an independent random sub-sample: for i = 1 to t, X′ ← sample(X, ψ) and Forest ← Forest ∪ iTree(X′, 0, l).
requirements.quote: X′ ←sample(X, ψ) 5: Forest ←Forest ∪iTree(X′, 0, l)

requirements.quote: It is assumed that anomaly labels are unavailable in the training stage.

routeInfo.why: The claim contract lists no code links and no repository was found or cloned; the paper (Liu, Ting & Zhou, 'Isolation Forest', ICDM 2008) released no reference implementation that this machine can obtain. The target claim (C1: AUC 0.85 on UCI Ionosphere with t=100 trees, psi=256) is nevertheless fully specified in the paper's own text: Alg. 2 (iTree construction with random attribute + random split in [min,max), height limit l = ceiling(log2 psi)), Alg. 3 (path-length adjustment for external nodes, h(x) = e + c(size)), and the scoring function s(x,psi) = 2^(-E(h(x))/c(psi)) with c(n) = 2H(n-1) - 2(n-1)/n. Nothing beyond this is needed, so the correct strategy is to reimplement the algorithm from the paper and the claim contract rather than hunt for author code. A third-party but algorithm-faithful implementation (sklearn.ensemble.IsolationForest, same authors' description in its docs) exists locally and will be used only as a cross-check / fallback, not as the authors' entrypoint.
routeInfo.est_runtime: Dominate cost is the Ionosphere download (~40 KB) and interpretation. Fitting 100 iTrees on 351 points with psi=256 takes well under 1 s single-threaded, matching the paper's reported 0.33 s train / 0.15 s eval. With a seed sweep (e.g. 20-50 repeats for a stable AUC and to characterise seed noise) the whole reproduction is ~1-3 minutes wall-clock on this 22-core CPU. Total well inside the 60-minute budget even including a from-scratch NumPy implementation and debugging.
blockers: no repository supplied and no code_links in the contract -> no authors' entrypoint to run
no GPU on this machine; irrelevant here since the whole pipeline is CPU-only and sub-second in the paper
Ionosphere is not bundled with scikit-learn; the run depends on being able to download ionosphere.data (or having it placed on disk). If the machine is offline this is the only hard blocker
Python 3.12 is fine - the paper's algorithm uses no deprecated frameworks (no Theano/Python2 issues); the only 'old' artefact is the data set, not the code

plan.approach: Because no author code is available and the paper fully specifies the algorithm, reproduce.py will implement Isolation Forest from Eqs. (1)-(2) and Algorithms 1-3: t=100 iTrees, psi=256 sub-samples drawn without replacement, height limit l=ceil(log2 psi)=8, random attribute/split selection, external-node path-length adjustment e+c(Size), and score s(x,psi)=2^(-E(h(x))/c(psi)). Data loading will fetch UCI Ionosphere, drop the class label and binary/constant columns to leave the 32 continuous features, map class 'bad' to anomaly 1 and 'good' to normal 0, and use the transductive protocol train=score=all 351 unlabelled instances. The fixed-seed run is the headline number for claim C1; a 10-seed sweep reports spread, and sklearn.ensemble.IsolationForest is used only as a cross-check/fallback, never as the authors' entrypoint. Success is AUC 0.85 +/- 0.05 on the fixed seed or seed mean, with total runtime a few seconds.
steps: Create working directories results/ and data/.
Write config.py with every value in the config object above.

Write data_loader.py: try requests.get(DATA_URL, timeout=30) and save to data/ionosphere.data; if that fails, call sklearn.datasets.fetch_openml(data_id=59) and save data/ionosphere.csv; parse the file, drop the class column, drop columns with nunique() <= 2 (the two binary features on Ionosphere), convert features to float64, and set y=1 for class in {'b','bad'} else 0. Assert X.shape == (351, 32), y.sum() == 126, and np.isfinite(X).all().

Write iforest.py: implement c(n)=2H(n-1)-2(n-1)/n with H(i)=ln(i)+0.5772156649 and c(1)=0; implement Node with is_external, size, q, p, left, right; implement build_itree(X, e, l, rng) where recursion stops if e >= l or n <= 1 or all rows identical; otherwise select a random attribute q with max > min, draw p = min + (max-min)*rng.random() in [min,max), and split left = X[:,q] < p, right = X[:,q] >= p; guard against empty splits by resampling up to 10 times, then make an external node if still empty.

Write iforest.py fit(X, t, psi, seed): create numpy.random.default_rng(seed); for each tree, draw psi indices without replacement with rng.choice(n, size=psi, replace=False) and call build_itree(X_sub, 0, ceil(log2 psi), rng).

Write iforest.py path_length(x, node, e=0): return e + c(node.size) at an external node; otherwise follow left if x[q] < p else right with e+1. Write anomaly_score(X): mean path lengths over all trees, then return 2 ** (-mean_h / c(psi)).
Write run_experiment.py: run_single_seed loads/uses X,y, fits the forest, times training and scoring separately, computes AUC with sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score(y, scores), and returns metrics.
Write run_experiment.py seed sweep: loop over seeds 0..9, call run_single_seed, and report mean, std, min, max, and total sweep runtime.

Write run_experiment.py sklearn cross-check: fit sklearn.ensemble.IsolationForest(n_estimators=t, max_samples=psi, random_state=seed, bootstrap=False), compute AUC from -score_samples(X) or decision_function(X), and record the value for comparison only.

Write reproduce.py with argparse: --smoke runs the tiny flow; --seed sets the headline seed (default 42); --seeds sets sweep count (default 10); --no-sklearn skips the cross-check. Default mode runs the full fixed-seed experiment, the seed sweep, optional sklearn check, and writes results/metrics.json.

Run the smoke test: python reproduce.py --smoke. This uses Ionosphere first 100 rows x first 8 features, t=5, psi=32, height_limit=5, seed=42, fits, scores, computes AUC, writes results/smoke_metrics.json, and exits 0 if all scores are finite and AUC in [0,1].

Run intermediate data checks: print X.shape, y mean, n_features, c(256), c(32), height_limit, max nodes per tree, and random-score AUC. Confirm shape (351,32), anomaly fraction ~0.36, c(256) ~= 10.2448, c(32) ~= 6.0849, height_limit=8, and max nodes per tree 511.

Run the full fixed-seed experiment with defaults: python reproduce.py. This trains t=100 iTrees, psi=256, seed=42 on all 351 instances, scores all 351 instances, and records AUC and train/eval/total times.

Run the 10-seed sweep in the same command and write results/metrics.json with fixed_seed.auc, fixed_seed.time_train_s, fixed_seed.time_eval_s, fixed_seed.time_total_s, seed_sweep.auc_mean, seed_sweep.auc_std, seed_sweep.auc_min, seed_sweep.auc_max, and sklearn_crosscheck.auc.

Validate pass criteria: fixed-seed AUC or seed mean must be within 0.85 +/- 0.05; the sklearn cross-check should be within 0.05 of the own implementation; single fit+score should be < 2 s and the 10-seed sweep < 30 s.

If the fixed-seed AUC is outside 0.80-0.90, debug in order: c(n) formula, height limit ceil(log2 psi), split direction x_q < p vs x_q >= p, sub-sampling without replacement, external-node adjustment e + c(Size), score normaliser c(psi), and score sign. Re-run smoke, then full.

Optional C6 sanity if time remains: generate 135 Gaussian points plus one anomaly, build 1000 trees with psi=128, and verify the anomaly's average path length is shorter than a normal point's average path length.
Finalize results/metrics.json and print a one-line summary: claim C1 target 0.85 +/- 0.05, observed fixed-seed AUC, observed seed-mean AUC, and passed true/false.
plan.smoke_test: Run `python reproduce.py --smoke`: load Ionosphere, take the first 100 instances and first 8 continuous features, fit iForest with t=5, psi=32, height_limit=5, seed=42, score those 100 points, compute AUC, assert all scores are finite and AUC is in [0,1], write results/smoke_metrics.json, and finish in under 2 s.
intermediate_checks: Data shape is (351, 32) after dropping the class and the two binary/constant Ionosphere columns; y.sum() is 126 (about 36% anomalies).
No NaN or infinite values in X; class labels are exactly 0/1 and match the 'good'/'bad' mapping.
c(256) ~= 10.2448 and c(32) ~= 6.0849; c(1)=0; the harmonic-number approximation uses 0.5772156649.

tolerance.why: The paper reports no spread for Ionosphere and no seed, so the band must be chosen before running. AUC is a bounded rank metric and iForest's own AUC only moves by ±0.0014–0.023 for large data sets (Section 5.2), but Ionosphere has only 351 instances with ~126 anomalies, so per-run randomness from sub-sampling and split-point selection is much larger; ±0.05 AUC (about ±6% relative) absorbs that run-to-run jitter while still rejecting a broken implementation, which would land near 0.5.

result.audit_summary:
The code is a faithful from-scratch NumPy implementation of iForest: c(n)=2H(n-1)-2(n-1)/n with the Euler harmonic approximation, l=ceil(log2 256)=8, sub-samples of psi=256 drawn without replacement, q

=p routing, e+c(Size) leaf adjustment, and s(x)=2^(-E(h(x))/c(psi)); all intermediate analytic values (c(256)=10.2448, 511-node bound, observed 215) check out. The experiment matches the C1 match target exactly in dataset (UCI Ionosphere, 351x32 after dropping the two binary attributes), metric (AUC via roc_auc_score), method (iForest, not a baseline) and the assumed transductive train=score=all-351 protocol of Table 3. Anti-cheat is clean: a grep for every paper Table 3/figure number in the five source files returns nothing, config.py stores only paper-specified hyper-parameters, the paper value enters only through an optional --target flag, and the headline number is computed from data with a uniform-random baseline (0.5219) and an independent scikit-learn cross-check (0.8475, diff 0.004) as sanity anchors. The clean re-run (exit 0, 3.9 s, data/ and results/ deleted first so the pipeline re-downloads UCI Ionosphere) reproduces AUC 0.8515 (seed 42) vs the paper's 0.85, well inside the pre-declared +/-0.05 band, with a 10-seed spread of 0.8476 +/- 0.0048 (min 0.8422, max 0.8553) and per-instance score range 0.36-0.71. Nothing was scaled down - full data set, full t=100/psi=256 - and the only free choices (seed, split-point distribution, transductive protocol, binary-attribute drop) are all disclosed in the assumption ledger (A1, A2, A5, A6). Times are wall-clock on a different machine than the paper's 2.3 GHz cluster, but timing is not the C1 target metric (AUC) and the discrepancy is explicitly disclosed.

requirement_check.evidence: iforest.IForest.score_samples returns 2.0 ** (-eh / c_factor(min(psi, n_train))) where eh is the mean path length across all trees (mean_path_lengths averages tree.path_lengths(x)). Directly Eq. (2) with n = psi.

iforest.c_factor implements 2*(log(n-1)+0.5772156649) - 2*(n-1)/n with EULER=0.5772156649 and c(1)=0; parameter_checks report c(2)=0.1544, c(32)=6.0849, c(256)=10.2448, matching the paper's analytic values.
IForest.height_limit = ceil(log2(psi)) = int(np.ceil(np.log2(256))) = 8; ITree.build stops when e >= height_limit. Observed max nodes/tree 215 <= 511 = 2^(l+1)-1.
fit() draws each tree's sub-sample with rng.choice(n, size=sub_size, replace=False) -> without replacement.
config.TREES = 100, passed to every run_single/sklearn call; metrics.json config records n_trees_t = 100.
config.PSI = 256, height limit 8 recorded; no psi change was needed for the C1 target.

ITree.build picks q among attributes with max>min and p = lo + (hi-lo)*rng.random(), i.e. p ~ Uniform[min_q, max_q); recursion halts on e>=l, n<=1, or no attribute with non-zero range. Minor undocumented deviation: if a draw yields an empty child the code retries up to 10 times before making the node a leaf (assumption A2/A3 territory); harmless here and consistent with the ledger.
left_mask = sub[:, q] < p, right_mask = ~left_mask (i.e. >= p); path_lengths uses go_left = vals < thr.
In ITree.path_lengths leaf handling: out[leaf_idx] = depth[leaf_idx] + c_factor(self.size[node[leaf_idx]]), i.e. e + c(Size).
fit() loops for _ in range(self.n_trees), re-drawing an independent sub-sample idx each iteration and building ITree.build(X[idx], height_limit, rng).
IForest.fit takes only X; run_single calls forest.fit(X) before any use of y, and y is only touched by roc_auc_score after score_samples.

data_loader._select_continuous keeps only columns with >2 distinct values; the parsed raw matrix has 34 columns and the retained matrix asserts shape (351, 32) with 126 'bad' labels - matching Table 2 (n=351, d=32, 36% anomalies).
sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score is used on the anomaly scores of all 351 instances; a uniform-random ranking cross-check gives 0.5219 (~0.5), confirming score direction.

contract.title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
contract.summary: Deep learning regression and classification tools typically do not capture model uncertainty, whereas Bayesian models do but at prohibitive computational cost. The paper casts dropout training in neural networks as approximate variational inference in deep Gaussian processes, yielding MC dropout: averaging T stochastic forward passes to estimate predictive mean and variance. On UCI regression benchmarks, notably Boston Housing, MC dropout improves test RMSE and predictive log-likelihood over VI and probabilistic back-propagation, achieving 2.97 ± 0.19 RMSE on Boston Housing in the 20-split setting.

routeInfo.why: The authors' repo is cloned and contains the entire experimental apparatus: experiment.py, net/net.py, and all UCI_Datasets directories with data.txt, the exact 20 train/test index splits, dropout_rates.txt, tau_values.txt, n_epochs/n_hidden configs, plus the authors' published result files (test_MC_rmse_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt etc.) for direct comparison. Nothing data- or weight-wise is missing (models are trained from scratch). What is broken is the runtime: the code targets Keras 2.2.0 on Theano 0.8.2 (README), Theano is unmaintained and not installable on Python 3.12, TF1.x/Keras 2.2 wheels do not exist for Python 3.12, and 9 of 11 Python files are Python-2 style. So we keep the authors' logic (architecture, dropout rates, epochs, tau/grid-search protocol, per-split train/val selection) but port the training/evaluation core to a modern framework and run the same splits.
routeInfo.est_runtime: Port work: ~20-30 min (rewrite net/net.py + experiment.py training/MC-dropout loop in a modern framework, keep split loading and grid-search logic). Runs (Boston Housing, 1x50 net, 400 epochs, batch 32, per-split grid over the repo's dropout_rates/tau_values, T MC forward passes): ~10-15 s per model fit on 22 CPU cores, so ~2-4 min per split with grid search. Full 20-split C1 protocol is ~40-80 min of compute, i.e. borderline-to-over the ~60 min total budget once the port is included.
routeInfo.scale_down_plan: Keep the exact released protocol but shrink along the split axis, not the model axis: evaluate the first 5 of the 20 released Boston Housing splits (index_train_*/index_test_*), same 1-hidden-layer/50-unit net, same dropout rates, same l=1e-2, same per-split train/val grid over tau, same 10x epochs (400), batch 32, Adam, T MC forward passes. Report mean test RMSE with standard error over 5 splits and state the split count explicitly. Secondary cheap confirmation on Yacht Hydrodynamics (N=308, <1 min/split) if time permits. Expected effect on the number: the point estimate should land near the released 2.83-2.97 range within a much wider error bar (SE roughly sqrt(20/5)~2x larger, i.e. +/-0.3-0.4 instead of +/-0.19); the qualitative claim (MC dropout beats VI, comparable-to-better than PBP 3.01) remains testable, but the printed +/-0.19 cannot be matched with 5 splits. If the port finishes fast, extend toward 10-20 splits; do not cut epochs or MC samples first, since those change the estimator itself.
blockers: code targets Theano 0.8.2 + Keras 2.2.0; Theano is dead and cannot be installed on Python 3.12
Keras 2.2.0 / TensorFlow 1.x have no wheels for Python 3.12 (and Keras 3 API differs: layer-level train-time dropout loops, .compile/.fit behaviour, model saving)
9 of 11 python files are Python-2 style (print statements, old import style) and need 2to3-style edits even before framework porting
no GPU on this machine; README launch command assumes device=gpu + float32 (not fatal: the UCI nets are tiny and the paper reports CPU-class runtimes, e.g. naval 276 s/split incl. BO)
protocol requires a per-split train/val split + grid search over dropout rate and tau before the final train, so per-split cost is much larger than a single 400-epoch fit

plan.approach: This is a partial_release reproduction: we keep the authors' released data and the exact 20 per-split train/test index files from https://github.com/yaringal/DropoutUncertaintyExps (bostonHousing/data/data.txt, index_train_i.txt, index_test_i.txt, dropout_rates.txt, tau_values.txt, n_epochs.txt, n_hidden.txt) and their grid-search-over-dropout-rate-and-tau protocol, but re-implement the 1-hidden-layer/50-unit dropout network plus the MC-dropout training/evaluation loop in PyTorch (CPU) because the original Keras 2.2.0 + Theano 0.8.2 stack and its Python-2 source cannot run on Python 3.12 (this is the single documented deviation from R13). For each of the first 5 of the 20 released Boston Housing splits we carve an 80/20 train/validation split from the training indices, grid-search dropout rate and tau by validation log-likelihood, set the L2 weight decay from the searched tau and l=1e-2 via the eq.(7) relation exactly as coded in net/net.py, train the final model for the fixed epoch budget (10x the base schedule, ~400 epochs, no early stopping) with Adam/batch-32, and evaluate test RMSE (inverse-transformed to original target units) and predictive log-likelihood with T=1000 MC-dropout stochastic forward passes. reproduce.py aggregates mean±standard-error over the 5 splits, writes results/metrics.json, and prints the authors' released per-split result files for direct comparison. The expected point estimate is ~2.83-2.97 (inside the 0.19 tolerance around C1=2.97) but with a roughly 2x wider standard error (5 of 20 splits), so the honest verdict is partially_reproduced.
steps: 1. Environment: verify python>=3.12, numpy/scipy/pandas/scikit-learn present, then `pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu` (CPU wheel) and `python -c "import torch;print(torch.__version__)"`. Do NOT attempt to install Theano/Keras 2.2/TF1 - they are uninstallable on 3.12 (documented blocker; deviation from R13).

Read experiment.py and net/net.py end-to-end; write down (in a notes file or docstring) the exact protocol: how the 80/20 train-val split is formed, how (dropout_rate, tau) are grid-searched and scored, how weight decay lambda is derived from tau/l/N, the exact epoch count and multiplier, and how RMSE and eq.(8) log-likelihood are computed. This dictation of the authors' logic is what the PyTorch port must mirror.
4. Parse the bostonHousing data dir config files and print them (dropout rates, tau values, n_epochs, n_hidden, n_splits, index_features, index_target) so the counts drive the grid size.
5. Write config.py with the values above (paper/assumption tags inline).
6. Write data_utils.py: load_data(split) -> (X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, X_test, y_test, scaler_y); standardize X and y on train statistics; verbose shapes. No torch import needed here.
7. Write model.py: DropoutRegressor(Q, hidden=50, p_in, p_out) with dropout before each weight layer; keep_dropout_at_eval flag.

8. Write mc_dropout.py: compute_lambda(tau,l,N) reading net/net.py's formula; train_model(...) (Adam lr=1e-3, batch 32, fixed epochs, shuffled); mc_predict(model, X, T=1000) -> mean, variance; rmse_inverse(y, yhat_mean, scaler_y); predictive_log_likelihood(...) per eq.(8)/net.py; grid_search(...) scoring by validation LL.

Write reproduce.py: iterate config.full_split_list, run grid search then final train then MC test eval, store per-split results, compute mean and SE = std/sqrt(n), set within_tolerance = |mean - 2.97| <= 0.19, dump results/metrics.json including split count, config snapshot, and the authors' released values.
10. Write compare_with_released.py to read the authors' results/*_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt files and print alongside ours.
11. Run the intermediate checks (see intermediate_checks) and fix any that fail before the full run.
12. Smoke test: `python reproduce.py --smoke` (split 0, 2 epochs, T=10, 1 grid point, 64 samples) - assert finite RMSE/LL, correct tensor shapes, <60 s.
13. Full run: `python reproduce.py --dataset bostonHousing --split-count 5` -> 5 splits x (grid search + 10x-epoch final train + T=1000 MC eval).
14. Inspect results/metrics.json: mean RMSE vs 2.97 with tolerance 0.19; compare to the authors' released 2.83/2.90; confirm the printed SE is ~2x the paper's because only 5 of 20 splits are used.
15. If budget remains after the 5-split Boston run, add a cheap secondary confirmation on Yacht Hydrodynamics (N=308), same protocol, and append it to metrics.json.

16. Write a short summary block into results/metrics.json stating the deviation (5/20 splits, grid-search instead of BO, PyTorch instead of Keras/Theano) and the resulting verdict (partially_reproduced).
plan.smoke_test: `python reproduce.py --smoke` runs only split 0 on the first 64 training rows for 2 epochs with T=10 MC forward passes and a single (dropout,tau) grid point; it asserts the data loader returns correctly shaped train/val/test arrays, the net has 751 parameters, training losses are finite and decreasing, MC predictions have shape (n_test,) with non-negative variance, and RMSE/log-likelihood are finite scalars. It writes results/smoke_metrics.json and must finish in under ~60 s, proving the full data->train->MC-eval->JSON flow before the expensive run.

Parameter count: 13*50+50 + 50*1+1 = 751 parameters; print and assert this matches the instantiated model.
