result.audit_summary: The reproduction targets the correct experiment: Boston Housing regression, RMSE in original units, using the authors' own released 20-split index files, a 1x50 ReLU dropout network, train-only standardisation, and MC-dropout averaging at test time. The value 2.9306 ± 0.2582 (5 splits) lies within the ±0.19 tolerance of the paper's 2.97 and is close to the authors' released 4000-epoch code anchor (2.9036) that the script parses from the repo rather than types in. Nothing is hard-coded or copied from the paper: paper_numbers_found_in_code is empty, all per-split numbers are produced by the clean re-run (identical to the recorded metrics.json), and the authors' result files are used only as a clearly-labelled external anchor. The main deviations are disclosed in the assumption ledger and in metrics notes: 5 of 20 splits (which is why the observed SE 0.2582 exceeds the paper's 0.19 — one split returns 4.07), grid search over the released grids instead of 40-iteration Spearmint BO, a single shared dropout rate rather than the paper's 0.05/0.005 pair, PyTorch instead of Keras/Theano, and T=10000 at test. These are framework/scale/hyperparameter-search substitutions that preserve the estimator; they do not make this a wrong experiment or an anti-cheat case, though R2 and R10 remain partial rather than fully met.

requirement_check.evidence: mc_dropout.DropoutNet is Linear(Q,H)->ReLU->Linear(H,1) with H read from the released data/n_hidden.txt (50); intermediate_check asserts 13*50+50+50+1=751 params and it passes.

Dropout is applied before every weight layer, but a single shared rate drawn from the released grid {0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1} is used for both layers instead of the paper's fixed pair (0.05 and 0.005). This matches the authors' net/net.py, but not the literal R2 text; per-split selected p varied (0.005/0.05/0.1/0.01/0.01).

weight_decay() = l^2(1-p)/(2 N tau) (net/net.py form of eq. 7); hand-checked in intermediate_checks and recorded per split (e.g. 1.09e-6 for N=364, tau=0.1); assumption A20 records the paper-vs-code formula choice.

Selection is by validation predictive log-likelihood, but the 40-iteration Spearmint BO was replaced by the authors' own 2018 exhaustive grid search over the released dropout_rates.txt x tau_values.txt (12 points per split). Disclosed as A18.
n_epochs = 40 (data/n_epochs.txt) * EPOCH_MULTIPLIER=10 = 400 epochs for every grid and final network, no early stopping; matches the C1 config and assumption A15.
config.BATCH_SIZE=32, torch.optim.Adam(lr=1e-3) with per-epoch shuffling (A6/A11).
config.LENGTH_SCALE=1e-2 used in the weight-decay computation.
mc_predict() runs T=10000 stochastic forward passes with dropout active at test time and averages them; RMSE computed in original target units after inverse standardisation.
predictive_log_likelihood() implements the eq. (8) MC estimate (released-code variant, +0.5 log tau); it is also the hyper-parameter selection criterion and is reported per split (mean -2.52).
Only splits 0-4 of the 20 released Boston Housing splits were run; SE over 5 splits = 0.2582 vs paper's 0.19. Disclosed in metrics notes, deviations list, and assumption A19.

data_utils reads the authors' released data.txt, index_features/target, and released per-split train/test index files (PBP splits), with train-only standardisation of X and y; overlap/coverage and 13-feature checks pass.
Fixed 400-epoch loop, no early stopping (config/notes); assumption A10.

Reimplemented in PyTorch CPU as an explicit port of the authors' Keras 2.2 / Theano 0.8 net/net.py (same architecture, dropout placement, weight decay, optimiser loop), because the released stack is not installable on Python 3.12. Disclosed deviation.

contract.title: Isolation Forest
contract.summary: Most anomaly detection methods profile normal instances and then flag deviations, which is costly and can be ineffective when anomalies are few and different. This paper introduces Isolation Forest (iForest), an ensemble of isolation trees that recursively and randomly partitions subsamples; anomalies tend to have shorter average path lengths and receive higher anomaly scores s(x,ψ)=2^{-E(h(x))/c(ψ)}. The authors report that iForest is competitive with or better than ORCA, LOF and Random Forests in AUC while being much faster, especially on large datasets, and that it works even when training contains only normal instances.

tolerance.why: The paper gives no std/CI for Table 3. Ionosphere is small (n=351, 36% anomalies), and iForest is stochastic through subsampling, attribute choice and split choice; the paper reports AUC to two decimals. An absolute band of 0.03 (about 3.5% relative on 0.85) allows reasonable seed/subsample variation while still rejecting a random detector AUC near 0.5. A 0.05 or larger band would be too loose for a rank-based AUC on this size of data.

requirements.stmt: Build each iTree as a proper binary tree: every internal node has a test of the form q < p and exactly two daughter nodes; every external node has no children and stores the size of the remaining data.
requirements.cite: Section 2, Definition Isolation Tree; Algorithm 2 lines 1-2 and 9-12
requirements.quote: An iTree is a proper binary tree, where each node in the tree has exactly zero or two daughter nodes.

requirements.stmt: Recursively partition a node until e >= l, |X| <= 1, or all data in X have the same values; then return an external node with Size = |X|.
requirements.quote: until either: (i) the tree reaches a height limit, (ii) |X| = 1 or (iii) all data in X have the same values.

requirements.stmt: Set the tree height limit to l = ceiling(log2 ψ).
requirements.quote: l = ceiling(log2 ψ), which is approximately the average tree height

requirements.stmt: For each iTree, draw a subsample X' of size ψ from X by random selection of instances without replacement.
requirements.cite: Section 3 ('sub-sampling is conducted by random selection of instances without replacement'); Algorithm 1 line 4
requirements.quote: Throughout this paper, sub-sampling is conducted by random selection of instances without replacement.

requirements.stmt: At each internal node, randomly select an attribute q uniformly from the list Q of attributes in the current X.
requirements.quote: we recursively divide X by randomly selecting an attribute q and a split value p

requirements.stmt: Select a split point p randomly between the maximum and minimum values of attribute q in the current X.
requirements.quote: randomly select a split point p from max and min values of attribute q in X

requirements.stmt: Partition the data into Xl = filter(X, q < p) and Xr = filter(X, q >= p).
requirements.quote: A test consists of an attribute q and a split value p such that the test q < p divides data points into Tl and Tr.

requirements.stmt: Build an ensemble of t iTrees; the default experiment value is t = 100.
requirements.quote: Unless otherwise specified, we shall use t = 100 as the default value in our experiment.

requirements.stmt: PathLength(x,T,e): if T is external, return e + c(T.size); otherwise compare x_a with T.splitValue, recurse left with e+1 if x_a < splitValue, else recurse right with e+1.
requirements.quote: When x is terminated at an external node, where Size > 1, the return value is e plus an adjustment c(Size).

requirements.stmt: Use c(n) = 2H(n-1) - 2(n-1)/n, where H(i) is the harmonic number and can be estimated by ln(i) + 0.5772156649.
requirements.quote: c(n) = 2H(n −1) −(2(n −1)/n), (1) where H(i) is the harmonic number

requirements.stmt: Compute anomaly score s(x,ψ) = 2^{-E(h(x))/c(ψ)}, where E(h(x)) is the average path length over the forest.
requirements.quote: s(x, n) = 2−E(h(x)) c(n) , (2) where E(h(x)) is the average of h(x) from a collection of isolation trees.

requirements.stmt: Use ψ = 256 as the default sub-sampling size unless otherwise specified.
requirements.quote: Unless otherwise specified, we use ψ = 256 as the default value for our experiment.

requirements.stmt: Compute AUC using anomaly labels only in the evaluation stage; labels must be unavailable during training.
requirements.quote: Anomaly labels are only available in the evaluation stage to compute the performance measure, AUC.

requirements.stmt: Remove all nominal and binary attributes and retain only continuous-valued attributes; for Ionosphere this yields d = 32.
For the high-dimensional irrelevant-attribute experiment only, apply a Kurtosis-based attribute selector per subsample before constructing each iTree.
requirements.quote: We use a simple statistical test, Kurtosis, to select an attribute subspace from the sub-sample before constructing each iTree.

routeInfo.why: The inspection record states plainly that no repository was found or given, and the claim contract lists no code links, so there is no author entrypoint to run or repair. The paper's algorithm, however, is fully specified in the contract itself (t=100 isolation trees, subsample size psi=256, height limit l=ceil(log2 psi), random continuous attribute q with split p uniform in [min(q),max(q)], score s(x,psi)=2^{-E(h(x))/c(psi)}, c(n)=2H(n-1)-2(n-1)/n), so the target can be rebuilt faithfully and cheaply from the paper: the iTree builder, the average-path-length function and the 2^{-E(h)/c} scorer are ~100 lines of numpy, and the evaluation protocol is Table 3 (train and score the same full dataset, AUC by rank statistic). All datasets are public (UCI/OpenML plus the ODDS mirrors of the KDDCUP99/benchmark collections), so nothing depends on author-released weights or configs. Hence reimplement from the paper and the claim contract rather than chase a release that does not exist.
routeInfo.est_runtime: Compute is trivial by modern standards: training costs O(t * psi * log psi) = 100 * 256 * 8 node evaluations per dataset (identical for every dataset, ~2e5 operations), and scoring costs O(t * n * log psi) with a vectorised per-level tree traversal. On 22 cores / 15.4 GB RAM / Python 3.12 + numpy that is: Ionosphere <1 s, Breastw/Arrhythmia/Pima <1 s each, Mammography/Satellite/Annthyroid a few seconds, Shuttle ~3 s, Mulcross ~15 s, ForestCover ~20 s, Http ~30-60 s - i.e. roughly 2-5 minutes for one full pass over all 8 Table 3 rows, ~10-25 minutes if each row is repeated 5-10x over seeds. Add a few minutes for download/parsing of the large mirrors. Total well inside the ~60-minute budget, with the dominant risk being download time, not compute.
routeInfo.scale_down_plan: Run in priority order so the target claim is never at risk. (1) Ionosphere (claim C1) first, exactly at paper defaults t=100, psi=256, no subsampling of the data, repeated over 5-10 seeds - this is a full-fidelity run and needs no scaling. (2) Then the other small/medium UCI rows (Breastw, Arrhythmia, Pima, Mammography, Satellite, Annthyroid, Shuttle) which cost seconds each. (3) Then the large rows (Mulcross, ForestCover, Http). If the KDDCUP99/ForestCover downloads are too slow or the mirror manifests differ from the paper's ref [14] preprocessing, drop C2/C3 or report them on the mirror data with the mismatch disclosed, and reduce large-dataset repeats from 10 to 1-3 - expected effect on the AUC number is small (iForest AUC on these sets is stable to roughly +/-0.01 across seeds at t=100, psi=256), but on n=567k with 0.4% attacks a single run can move AUC by a few 1e-3, so the reduced-repeat numbers would be reported as single-run with an explicit caveat. Also, if total time runs short, cap the whole study at the 4 cheapest datasets rather than truncating Ionosphere.
blockers: no repository released or linked anywhere in the contract - nothing to clone, no entrypoint to run

Table 3 protocol is train-and-evaluate on the same full dataset (no held-out split), which inflates AUC versus a clean split; the contract flags this and it must be reproduced as stated, with the caveat recorded

dataset downloads (KDDCUP99 mirrors and ForestCover are the large ones) must succeed; no network access would drop C2/C3/C4 and leave the small UCI rows reproducible

plan.approach: Reimplement iForest from the paper because no author repository exists: build an isolation tree ensemble with t=100 trees, subsample psi=256 without replacement, height limit l=ceil(log2 psi)=8, random continuous attribute q, uniform split p in [min(q),max(q)), and score s(x,psi)=2^{-E(h(x))/c(psi)}. Use the ODDS .mat mirrors for Ionosphere and the other Table 3 datasets so preprocessing (e.g., Ionosphere d=32) matches the paper. For Table 3, train and score each full dataset without a held-out split, repeat over 10 seeds, and report mean AUC with std. Entrypoint reproduce.py runs a smoke test, then C1 (Ionosphere) and optionally all claims, writing results/metrics.json; C1 is judged against 0.85 +/- 0.03.
steps: Create project layout: ./config.py, ./iforest.py, ./data.py, ./evaluate.py, ./reproduce.py, ./data/raw/, ./results/. Verify numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, and requests are importable; pip install only if missing.
Write config.py with the hyperparameters and dataset metadata above, including claim IDs, paper AUC values, expected shapes, anomaly rates, seeds, and tolerance.

Write iforest.py: implement c(n) with exact harmonic sum for n<=1000 and the paper's approximation otherwise; implement IsolationTree.build(X, depth, rng) with stopping rules depth>=height_limit, len(X)<=1, or no split possible; store q, p, left, right, size. Implement IsolationForest.fit(X) drawing min(psi,n) rows without replacement per tree. Implement score_batch(X) with a per-tree stack of (node, sample_indices, depth) for vectorized traversal, returning 2**(-E_h/c(effective_psi)).

Write data.py: for each requested claim, download the ODDS .mat file to data/raw/{odds_name}.mat with requests (timeout 120s); load with scipy.io.loadmat and locate keys X and y; flatten y and set y=1 for anomaly; verify X.shape == (n,d) against config. For Ionosphere, if ODDS fails, fall back to UCI ionosphere.data and drop binary/nominal columns to d=32.
Write evaluate.py: compute AUC with sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score(y_true, scores); aggregate per-seed AUCs into mean, std, min, max, and list.
Write reproduce.py: CLI flags --smoke, --claim, --all, --out, --n-repeats, --seed. Default action prints the config and runs C1 if no flag.
Run the smoke test: python reproduce.py --smoke. Confirm it writes results/smoke_metrics.json with a finite AUC and exits 0.

Run intermediate checks on Ionosphere: assert X.shape==(351,32), y.sum()==126, c(256) in [10.2,10.3], all tree depths <=8, every external node size >=1, mean path length(y=1) < mean path length(y=0), scores in [0,1], and random-score AUC near 0.5.

Run full C1: python reproduce.py --claim C1 --n-repeats 10. Train t=100 trees with psi=256 on all 351 Ionosphere rows, score the same rows, and report mean AUC over 10 seeds. Compare mean AUC to 0.85 with absolute tolerance 0.03 and write within_tolerance to results/metrics.json.
If C1 passes, run the remaining small/medium claims in order C7 Breastw, C8 Arrhythmia, C6 Mammography, C5 Shuttle with 10 seeds each; each should take seconds to minutes.
If time and network permit, run the large claims C4 Mulcross, C3 ForestCover, C2 Http with 3-10 seeds (start with 3, increase if runtime is low). Record actual runtimes and data-source hashes.

Write results/metrics.json containing for every completed claim: claim_id, dataset, n, d, anomaly_rate, paper_value, mean_auc, std_auc, per_seed_auc, n_seeds, tolerance, within_tolerance, runtime_sec, odds_url, and the full config. Mark failed/unattempted claims as not_run with the reason.

target.statement: iForest achieves the reported AUC on Ionosphere using default parameters.
target.table_ref: Table 3, row Ionosphere, column AUC/iForest

tolerance.why: The paper gives no std/CI for Table 3. Ionosphere is small (n=351, 36% anomalies), and iForest is stochastic through subsampling, attribute choice and split choice; the paper reports AUC to two decimals. An absolute band of 0.03 (about 3.5% relative on 0.85) allows reasonable seed/subsample variation while still rejecting a random detector AUC near 0.5. A 0.05 or larger band would be too loose for a rank-based AUC on this size of data.

result.audit_summary: The re-implementation matches the paper's Algorithm 1-3 for Table 3: t=100 iTrees, psi=256 without-replacement subsampling, height limit 8, uniform attribute and uniform split-point selection, external nodes storing |X|, PathLength with c(n)=2H(n-1)-2(n-1)/n, and score s(x,psi)=2^{-E(h(x))/c(psi)}, with labels used only in the sklearn rank-AUC. The primary target C1 (Ionosphere 351x32, 126 anomalies = 35.9%) is reproduced at 0.8493 +/- 0.0079 over 10 seeds versus the paper's 0.85, comfortably inside the +/-0.03 tolerance, and the clean re-run reproduces the identical deterministic per-seed values, so nothing is hard-coded or echoed (paper_numbers_found_in_code is empty). The other obtainable rows also agree: ForestCover 0.8798 vs 0.88, Shuttle 0.9971 vs 1.00, Mammography 0.8694 vs 0.86, Breastw 0.9874 vs 0.99, Arrhythmia 0.7919 vs 0.80, each with the contract's (n, d, anomaly count) asserted in code. C2 (Http) and C4 (Mulcross) are correctly reported not_run because those exact datasets are not publicly distributable; this is missing data, disclosed rather than substituted with a fabricated number. Residual risk is small and confined to documented assumptions: the Table 3 train-and-score-the-same-rows protocol (A6) and the constant-attribute edge case (A4, ablated at <=0.01 AUC); the intermediate structural checks (max depth 8, c(256)=10.2487, anomalies have shorter mean path 9.69 vs 12.70, random-score AUC ~0.49) all pass.

requirement_check.evidence: iforest.py defines _Node(feature, threshold, left, right, size) with is_external = (feature is None); _grow returns either _leaf(n) or _Node(q, p, left, right, None), i.e. exactly one test and two distinct daughters per internal node. reproduce.tree_depths asserts node.left/right are non-None and distinct, and that external nodes have size>=1 and no children; first-seed audit reports 7327 external nodes, min external size 1, max depth 8.

_grow stops and returns an external node when e >= height_limit or n <= 1, and when the drawn attribute cannot separate the node (hi[q] <= lo[q], ledger A4). The paper's third stopping case (all values identical) is subsumed; the extra A4 early-stop is a documented edge-case assumption whose two-seed ablation moves AUC by <=0.0100 (Ionosphere 0.8521 vs 0.8423, Shuttle 0.9975 vs 0.9974, ForestCover 0.8790 vs 0.8690).
config.HEIGHT_LIMIT = ceil(log2 256) = 8, and IsolationForest.height_limit = ceil(log2(max_samples)) = 8; checks.json contains height_limit_is_ceil_log2_psi = true and max_tree_depth = 8 <= 8.
IsolationForest.fit draws psi = min(max_samples, n) rows per tree via rng.choice(n, size=psi, replace=False) (without replacement); every reported dataset has n > 256 so psi = 256.
In _grow: q = int(self.rng.integers(self.n_features)) — a uniform draw over the attributes present in the current node's X (all columns are retained down the tree).

p = self.rng.uniform(lo[q], hi[q]) with lo/hi = per-node min/max of attribute q (numpy uniform is [lo,hi)); a bounded retry then deterministic midpoint fallback only guards against degenerate (empty-child) draws, which cannot occur for lo<hi.

left_mask = X[:, q] < p; Xl = X[left_mask], Xr = X[~left_mask], exactly q

=p right.
config.N_ESTIMATORS = 100 and every fit uses it (reproduce.build_and_score passes config.N_ESTIMATORS); metrics.json config records n_estimators=100 for all claims.

IsolationTree.path_lengths implements Algorithm 3: external node -> e + c(node.size); otherwise X[idx, feature] < threshold ? recurse left with e+1 : recurse right with e+1 (vectorised with an explicit stack while preserving the e+1 recursion).
c(n) = 2*H(n-1) - 2*(n-1)/n with exact harmonic sum for n<=1000 and ln(i)+0.5772156649 beyond; c(256) = 10.2487 (paper's approximation gives 10.244, 0.05% apart), c(0)=c(1)=0, checks confirm.
score_samples returns 2.0 ** (-mean_path_length / c(psi)) where mean_path_length averages PathLength over all trees and psi = min(256,n); audit shows all scores finite and in (0,1].
config.MAX_SAMPLES = 256, used as max_samples for every claim (psi=256 for all reported datasets since n>256).

Training consumes only X (IsolationForest.fit(X) and Tree.fit(X[rows])); y is loaded separately and used only in evaluate.auc -> sklearn roc_auc_score. Random-score control AUC ~0.494 (smoke) / 0.463 (Ionosphere) confirms AUC is computed from scores, not labels.

data.drop_non_continuous keeps only columns with >2 distinct values; Ionosphere loads 351x33 from the ODDS/pyod mirror, one binary column is dropped -> (351, 32) with 126 anomalies, asserted against the contract shape; Shuttle/ForestCover/Mammography/Breastw/Arrhythmia use only continuous attributes (9/10/6/9/274).

Kurtosis attribute selection is explicitly disabled for the Table 3 protocol: config/iforest carry no Kurtosis step and metrics.json records "kurtosis_attribute_selection": false; the selector is only referenced in the ledger as a Section 5.3 option, not implemented for these claims.

divergence_causes: randomness (subsampling, attribute draw and split point are stochastic; the reported value is a 10-seed mean with std 0.0079 for C1)
paper_underspecified (A1 seed/RNG control, A2 split-point distribution, A4 constant-attribute behaviour, A6 train/evaluate-on-same-data protocol for Table 3)

contract.title: Bag of Tricks for Efficient Text Classification
contract.summary: The paper addresses efficient text classification, where deep neural models achieve strong accuracy but are slow to train and test. It proposes fastText, a linear model with a rank constraint, bag-of-words/n-gram features, hierarchical softmax, and asynchronous SGD on CPUs. On sentiment and tag-prediction benchmarks fastText is on par with deep-learning classifiers while being orders of magnitude faster; the target AG News test accuracy with h=10 and bigrams is 92.5%.

routeInfo.why: The authors' complete implementation of the exact system claimed is public and cloned: src/ is the C++ fastText whose supervised mode ('./fasttext supervised -dim 10 -wordNgrams 2 -epoch 5 -lr ...') is precisely the configuration of C1, and the repo ships the authors' own reproduction script for Table 1 (classification-results.sh), which downloads the Zhang et al. 8-dataset release (incl. AG News 120k train / 7.6k test) and trains/evaluates every row. No weights are needed (training is from scratch), the paper's hyperparameters (h=10, bigrams, 5 epochs, lr in {0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5}, 20 CPU threads) are fully specified, no GPU is required, and the host's 22 CPU cores match the paper's 20-thread CPU setup, so training costs seconds-to-minutes. What remains is environment plumbing rather than missing science: the Linux/POSIX build path and the dataset download. Fallback if the native build cannot be made to work on Windows is to install the same code as a prebuilt wheel (pip fasttext-wheel / fasttext) or, worst case, use the authors' own PyTorch EmbeddingBag fastText model (python/doc/examples/FastTextEmbeddingBag.py) as the training engine, with the caveat that the latter is a re-implementation and would downgrade the verdict to partially_reproduced.
routeInfo.est_runtime: ~10-20 min total: toolchain/wheel setup 2-5 min (skipped if a prebuilt wheel is used), AG News download + format conversion 1-3 min, 4 lr runs x 5 epochs (~1-2 s/epoch on 20 of 22 cores) + test prediction on 7.6k examples (~seconds each) = ~2-5 min, final model retrain + test <1 min
blockers: Host is Windows 11: classification-results.sh is a bash script and the Makefile/`make` path assumes a POSIX shell plus g++/clang++ - neither is guaranteed present; needs MinGW/MSYS2, WSL or CMake+MSVC

setup.py hard-codes '-O3 -funroll-loops -pthread -march=native' extra compile args, which MSVC rejects, so 'pip install .' from source on Windows needs MinGW or a prebuilt wheel (fasttext-wheel) instead
'make' uses -march=native -std=c++17; fine on modern gcc/clang, irrelevant if a wheel is used
No GPU on the host - not a blocker: the paper's fastText rows are CPU-only (20 threads) and AG News trains in ~1 s/epoch
Network access to the dataset download URLs cannot be assumed; a mirror (HF ag_news) plus a short format converter covers this

plan.approach: The paper's exact system is the authors' own fastText C++ supervised trainer, and the repo ships classification-results.sh which downloads the Zhang et al. 8-dataset release and trains/evaluates every Table 1 row, so the plan is plumbing rather than re-implementation: get a working fasttext engine, get AG News in `__label__N` format, then run the authors' configuration `-dim 10 -wordNgrams 2 -epoch 5 -lr <lr> -thread 20`. A thin reproduce.py drives everything with the Python binding (fasttext-wheel on Windows, native build or `make` when a POSIX toolchain exists), reconstructs the missing validation split (10% of the 120k train set, assumption A4) to pick lr from {0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5}, then retrains on the full training set and evaluates on the official 7.6k test set. The same driver also emits the no-bigram C2 row for free. Only results/metrics.json is written by us; all training/eval numbers come from the authors' binary or its official Python binding, and the fallback to the authors' PyTorch EmbeddingBag example is explicitly flagged as a re-implementation. Everything is CPU-only with 20 threads, matching the paper.
steps: Environment probe: print python version, os.cpu_count(), total RAM, and shutil.which for make/g++/clang/cmake; confirm the cloned repo path and record `git rev-parse HEAD`.

Read the authors' classification-results.sh and classification-example.sh to copy their exact dataset URLs and argument list for the AG News row; do not edit them. If a POSIX bash + make are available, running classification-results.sh directly is the preferred path and reproduce.py only parses/wraps its output.

Build/find the engine via fasttext_engine.py: try `import fasttext`; else `pip install fasttext-wheel` (prebuilt, Windows-safe); else native `make`/`pip install .`; else fall back to the authors' PyTorch EmbeddingBag example and mark the run as a re-implementation.

Download AG News with prepare_data.py (authors' URL first, then Zhang et al. CSV / HF mirror) and convert to `__label__1..4 <tokens>` lines; write data/ag_news.full.train (120k), data/ag_news.test (7.6k) and, with a fixed seed, data/ag_news.train (108k) + data/ag_news.valid (12k).

Smoke test (see smoke_test): train on 2k lines, 1 epoch, dim 10, wordNgrams 2, verify the returned (N, P@1, R@1), verify `test` on the 1k test subset, and verify a stub results/metrics.json round-trips.

Intermediate checks before the full run: line counts 120000/7600 (full train/test) and 108000/12000 (search/valid), 4-class balance printout, label set == {__label__1..4}, vocabulary and bigram-hash collision counts, and a 1-epoch unigram sanity baseline well above the 25% chance level.

lr search: for lr in {0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5} run the authors' trainer on data/ag_news.train with -dim 10 -wordNgrams 2 -epoch 5 -lr <lr> -thread 20 -minCount 1, evaluate on data/ag_news.valid, keep all four validation accuracies.

Final C1 run: pick the argmax-lr and retrain on the full 120k data/ag_news.full.train with the same flags, then run the authors' test command on data/ag_news.test (7.6k) and record P@1 as a percentage.
C2 run (cheap): repeat the final training with -wordNgrams 1 at the selected lr and evaluate on data/ag_news.test.

Write results/metrics.json in the contract's shape: {claim_id, dataset, split, metric, value, unit, target_value, tolerance, passed, config_used, lr_search_results, validation_accuracy, test_examples, engine ('fasttext-wheel' | 'native build' | 'EmbeddingBag re-implementation'), git_hash, runtime_seconds} for C1 and a secondary entry for C2.
Report: the C1 accuracy with |acc - 92.5| <= 1.0 pass/fail, the selected lr, the engine provenance, and any deviation entry (e.g., bucket=10M instead of A3's 100M).

Runs in well under a minute.

Class balance: 4 labels, each ~25% in train and test (AG News is exactly balanced); print counts before training.
Label vocabulary: sorted label set equals {__label__1,__label__2,__label__3,__label__4}; no row lacks a label prefix.
Feature sanity: report dictionary word count and the fraction of the 10M bin space probed by bigrams (fastText verbose=2 prints these), and confirm minn=maxn=0 so no character n-grams leak in.

Sanity baseline: unigram fastText (wordNgrams=1, 1 epoch, lr=0.1) on the 108k search set should reach roughly 85-90% on the validation set, comfortably above the 25% chance level; if it is near chance the data conversion (labels/tokens) is wrong.

plan.budget_plan: Of a ~45 min budget: 2 min environment probe + engine setup attempts (extended only if a native build is needed), 1-3 min data download/convert/verify, 1 min smoke test, 2 min intermediate checks plus the unigram baseline, 7-8 min for the 4-point lr grid (4 x 5 epochs on 108k ~ 10-20 s each plus validation eval), ~1 min for the final retrain on 120k and the 7.6k test pass, ~1 min for the no-bigram C2 run, 2-3 min to write results/metrics.json and the report. Total ~15-20 min, leaving >2x margin; the only unbounded step is the toolchain/wheel install, which is capped at 5 min before switching to the EmbeddingBag fallback.

result.audit_summary: The match target C1 (AG News, h=10, bigrams, test accuracy vs paper 92.5%) is genuinely reproduced: the clean re-run trains from scratch on the full Zhang et al. 120k/7.6k AG News split with the official facebookresearch/fastText 0.9.2 trainer (fasttext-wheel binding, no re-implementation) and reports 92.3447% (mean over 5 seeds, std 0.09), i.e. 0.16 pt below the paper and well inside the 1.0-pt tolerance; C2 without bigrams gives 91.3605% vs 91.5%. No number is hard-coded, echoed from the paper, or computed on the wrong split: the test set is untouched, learning rate is chosen by a grid search on a 10% train holdout with duplicate articles grouped to avoid leakage, and the ledger shows an explicit grep confirming no target numbers ('92.5','91.5',...) appear in the source. The main fidelity deviation is that loss='softmax' (full softmax) is used rather than the paper's hierarchical softmax (R4/R12), and metrics.json consequently mislabels 'hierarchical_softmax': true; for a 4-class problem this is accuracy-immaterial but should be corrected in reporting. Other minor, disclosed deviations are bucket=10M instead of the paper's 100M for unigram+bigram features (assumption A15, matching the authors' own script) and thread=20 (paper) vs 4 (authors' script). The residual 0.15-pt gap is consistent with fastText's non-seedable asynchronous SGD noise and the paper-underspecified lr/validation/tokenization choices (A1, A4, A5), not with an implementation error.

config.py LOSS="softmax" selects fastText's full softmax, NOT hierarchical softmax ('hs'); the metrics.json field 'hierarchical_softmax': true is therefore mislabelled. With k=4 labels the accuracy impact is negligible (92.34 vs paper 92.5), but the paper's Huffman-tree trick is not exercised.
thread=20 and the clean-rerun log shows the linearly decaying lr ('lr: 0.030040 ... lr: 0.000000') characteristic of fastText's async multi-CPU SGD.
dim=10, epoch=5, lr grid [0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5] searched on a held-out 10% validation split; selected lr=0.25 with valid acc 92.0361 vs 91.9944 for 0.1.

contract.summary: WebLoop addresses functional Web generation by jointly learning Generator, Critic, and Refiner roles within a shared policy, where the Critic is execution-free at inference but receives execution-derived credit during training. The method trains the Critic with requirement-level discriminability labels and downstream refinement helpfulness, then optimizes all three roles with role-specific group-relative GRPO. With Qwen3.5-9B, WebLoop reaches 41.5 Overall on WebRise and 38.9% accuracy on WebGen-Bench, improving the base model by 11.3 and 15.4 points respectively.

tolerance.why: Rule 2: WebRise Overall is an accuracy-like percentage metric on a test set of 442 tasks (fewer than 2,000 examples, so Rule 2 does not apply). Rule 3 applies: it is a bounded score on a smaller set, so the tolerance is 2.0 absolute points. The paper reports no std over repeated runs, so Rule 1 does not apply.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify the exact prompt templates for Generator, Critic, and Refiner; it only says complete role-specific prompts are in Sec. D, which is not included in the provided text.
assumptions.quote: The Critic inspects an imperfect implementation against the task requirements and produces requirement-level judgments and repair guidance.
assumptions.chosen: Reconstruct prompts from the described conditioning contexts and output formats, ensuring the Critic outputs requirement-level judgments and repair guidance and the Generator/Refiner output complete HTML.
options: Reconstruct prompts from the described conditioning contexts and output formats
Use generic instruction prompts without requirement-level structured output
Request the authors' released prompts upon acceptance
assumptions.rationale: The paper states the Critic predicts whether each explicit requirement is satisfied and provides repair guidance, and the Generator/Refiner produce complete HTML implementations; these constraints are sufficient to build faithful prompts even without Sec. D.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify how to parse the Critic's free-form output into requirement-level binary predictions z_hat_j,q for discriminability computation.
assumptions.quote: Critiques that cannot be parsed into the required requirement-level judgments receive the minimum Critic reward and do not instantiate downstream refinement branches.
assumptions.chosen: Use a structured output format enforced by the prompt, and treat unparseable critiques as minimum Critic reward with no downstream refinement branches, as stated in Appendix A.2.
options: Use a structured output format (e.g., JSON or per-requirement labels) enforced by the prompt
Use a separate parser model or heuristic string matching
Treat unparseable critiques as minimum reward and skip downstream refinement
assumptions.rationale: The paper explicitly says critiques that cannot be parsed into required requirement-level judgments receive the minimum Critic reward and do not instantiate downstream refinement branches, so a structured parser is the faithful choice.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify the exact browser automation stack, headless browser version, or timeout handling beyond the per-example hard timeout of 2,400 seconds.
assumptions.quote: Browser execution is parallelized independently from model rollout, with up to 72 concurrent evaluations and a per-example hard timeout of 2,400 seconds.
assumptions.chosen: Use Playwright with Chromium, as it is the most common modern browser automation stack for executable Web evaluation and supports the required interaction and assertion execution.
options: Use Playwright with Chromium
Use Selenium with Chrome
Use Puppeteer with Chromium
assumptions.rationale: The paper only says browser execution is parallelized with up to 72 concurrent evaluations and a 2,400-second timeout; the specific stack is not pinned, so a standard headless Chromium automation library is the conventional choice.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify the exact GRPO clipping parameter εclip, the normalization epsilon εnorm, or the number of optimization epochs per rollout batch.
assumptions.quote: Our implementation is built on verl with an FSDP2 actor and asynchronous vLLM rollout workers.
assumptions.chosen: Use common GRPO defaults: εclip = 0.2, εnorm = 1e-8, and one epoch per rollout batch, following the verl framework defaults.
options: Use common GRPO defaults: εclip = 0.2, εnorm = 1e-8, one epoch per batch
Tune these on a validation set
Use the values from the verl framework defaults
assumptions.rationale: The paper states the implementation is built on verl with FSDP2 actor and asynchronous vLLM rollout workers, so verl's default GRPO hyperparameters are the most faithful convention when the paper omits them.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify how the initial-state contract and Interaction Contract Graph are represented or executed for the 2,880 training tasks, beyond saying they follow WebRISE.
assumptions.quote: Following WebRISE (Meng et al., 2026), each task is associated with an Interaction Contract Graph Gx that specifies browser interactions and functional assertions.
assumptions.chosen: Reuse the WebRISE ICG format and executor directly, since the paper says the construction follows WebRISE and uses the same browser executor for evaluation.
options: Reuse the WebRISE ICG format and executor directly
Reimplement the ICG format from the WebRISE paper
Use a simplified state-transition format
assumptions.rationale: The paper explicitly follows WebRISE for the Interaction Contract Graph and uses the same browser executor for WebRise evaluation, so reusing the WebRISE format is the most faithful and lowest-risk choice.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify the exact task batch size scheduling, gradient accumulation, or whether the 64-task batch is split across GPUs.
assumptions.quote: Training uses 3K text-conditioned Web generation tasks with a task batch size of 64.
assumptions.chosen: Use task batch size 64 with gradient accumulation as needed to fit the available hardware, keeping the effective batch size at 64.
options: Use task batch size 64 with gradient accumulation to fit memory
Use a smaller batch and scale the learning rate
Use the largest batch that fits without accumulation
assumptions.rationale: The paper states a task batch size of 64, so preserving the effective batch size is important for faithful reproduction; gradient accumulation is a standard implementation detail when memory is limited.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify the exact evaluation protocol for WebRise beyond using the same Interaction Contract Graph and browser executor, including how Overall is computed from T, Re, and Ri.
assumptions.quote: WebRise contains 442 tasks and reports transition validity T , explicit requirement coverage Re, implicit requirement coverage Ri, and their average Overall score.
assumptions.chosen: Compute Overall as the average of T, Re, and Ri, following the WebRISE benchmark definition, since the paper says WebRise reports these metrics and their average Overall score.
options: Compute Overall as the average of T, Re, and Ri
Use the WebRISE official Overall definition
Weight T, Re, and Ri differently
assumptions.rationale: The paper explicitly states WebRise reports transition validity T, explicit requirement coverage Re, implicit requirement coverage Ri, and their average Overall score, so the average is the stated definition.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify how to handle tasks where no valid imperfect draft exists beyond saying they contribute only initial-generation samples.
assumptions.quote: If Y− x is empty, no Critic or Refiner branch is expanded for that task.
assumptions.chosen: Skip Critic and Refiner branches for those tasks and include only Generator samples in the batch, as stated in Appendix A.2.
options: Skip Critic and Refiner branches for those tasks and include only Generator samples in the batch
Resample until a valid imperfect draft is found
Use the best valid draft even if it fully solves the task
assumptions.rationale: The paper explicitly says if Y-_x is empty, no Critic or Refiner branch is expanded for that task, so this is the faithful behavior.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify the exact seed or random initialization for the policy, browser evaluation, or data ordering.
assumptions.quote: Unless otherwise stated, controlled comparisons use the same backbone initialization, training-task distribution, browser evaluation infrastructure, and metric computation.
assumptions.chosen: Use a fixed seed for reproducibility and document it, since the paper reports no variance across seeds and controlled comparisons use the same initialization.
options: Use a fixed seed for reproducibility
Use multiple seeds and report variance
Use the default seed of the training framework
assumptions.rationale: The paper says controlled comparisons use the same backbone initialization and training-task distribution, implying a fixed setup; a fixed seed is the standard convention for reproducible RL training.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify how the Critic's repair guidance is formatted or how the Refiner consumes it beyond conditioning on the critique.
assumptions.quote: The Critic inspects an imperfect implementation against the task requirements and produces requirement-level judgments and repair guidance.
assumptions.chosen: A combination of requirement-level verdicts and free-form guidance, matching the paper's description that the Critic produces requirement-level judgments and repair guidance.
options: Free-form natural language repair suggestions
Structured per-requirement fix suggestions
A combination of requirement-level verdicts and free-form guidance
assumptions.rationale: The paper states the Critic produces requirement-level judgments and repair guidance, and Fig. 2 shows both diagnosis scores and fix suggestions, so a combined format is faithful.

Rule 3 applies to a bounded score on a smaller set and gives 2.0 absolute points. The original tolerance incorrectly applied Rule 2 and narrowed the value to 1.0.

match_target.why: C1 is the paper's headline central result on the primary benchmark (WebRise Overall with Qwen3.5-9B), and it is the cheapest target because the 9B model is the smallest backbone used for all controlled experiments and the WebRise Text-modality evaluation is the main reported setting. requirements.stmt: Use a shared policy that sequentially instantiates Generator, Critic, and Refiner roles under different conditioning contexts.
requirements.quote: WebLoop uses a shared policy πθ to instantiate three roles under different conditioning contexts.

requirements.stmt: The Generator produces a complete initial HTML implementation from the task description and requirements.
requirements.quote: The Generator maps the task to a complete initial HTML implementation

requirements.stmt: The Critic must be execution-free at inference: it receives only task requirements and source code, never browser results, requirement labels, or execution traces.
requirements.quote: browser results, requirement labels, and execution traces are never exposed to the Critic as input.

requirements.stmt: The Refiner conditions on the task, current implementation, and critique to produce a complete revised HTML implementation.
requirements.quote: The Refiner conditions on the task, the current implementation, and the critique to generate a complete revised HTML implementation.

requirements.stmt: Both initial and refined implementations are evaluated by the same browser environment using the Interaction Contract Graph, returning transition validity, explicit/implicit requirement coverage, and requirement-level labels.
requirements.quote: Executing a page y returns E(y; Gx) = (T (y), Re(y), Ri(y), z(y))

requirements.stmt: The page-level execution reward must be rweb(y) = 0.50 T(y) + 0.25 Re(y) + 0.25 Ri(y).

requirements.cite: Section 3.1, Critique-conditioned branching; Appendix A.2, Eq. 12-13
requirements.stmt: Select the median-reward candidate among valid but imperfect initial implementations as the shared base draft yb; if none exists, the task contributes only initial-generation samples.
requirements.quote: we select the median-reward candidate among valid but imperfect implementations as the shared base draft yb.

requirements.stmt: Compute diagnostic discriminability as balanced class-wise accuracy D(cj) = afail(cj) + apass(cj) - 1, with single-class rescaling to [-1, 1].
requirements.quote: D(cj ) = afail(cj ) + apass(cj ) − 1

requirements.stmt: Compute retrospective helpfulness as the mean execution reward of nr refinements conditioned on the critique minus the base draft reward.
requirements.quote: H(cj ) = 1 nr nrX k=1 rweb (y(2) j,k) − rweb(yb).

requirements.cite: Section 3.2, Eq. 7; Appendix A.1, Critic schedule
requirements.stmt: Use staged Critic credit: discriminability only for the first 15 updates, then H(cj) + λD(cj) with λ = 0.2.
requirements.quote: r(m) crit (cj ) = D(cj ), m ≤ 15, H(cj ) + λD(cj ), m > 15

requirements.stmt: Construct role-specific comparison groups: Generator outputs under the same task, Critic outputs under the same base draft, Refiner outputs under the same critique.
requirements.quote: Generator outputs are compared under the same task, Critic outputs under the same base draft, and Refiner outputs under the same critique.

requirements.stmt: Compute group-relative advantage as Ao = (r(o) - μg(o)) / (σg(o) + εnorm).
requirements.quote: Ao = r(o) − μg(o) σg(o) + ϵnorm

requirements.stmt: Merge Generator, Critic, and Refiner samples into a single optimization batch and optimize the shared policy with the clipped GRPO objective.
requirements.quote: Generator, Critic, and Refiner samples are merged into a single optimization batch O.

requirements.cite: Section 4.1, Models and training; Appendix A.1, Rollout structure
requirements.stmt: For each task, sample ng = 3 initial generations, nc = 3 critiques for the selected imperfect draft, and nr = 3 refinements per critique, yielding 12 executable Web candidates per rollout.
requirements.quote: we sample three initial generations, three critiques for the selected imperfect draft, and three refinements per critique, yielding 12 executable Web candidates per rollout.

requirements.stmt: Train with GRPO using learning rate 1e-6, no explicit KL penalty, temperature 0.7, top-p 1.0, and maximum prompt/response length 16,384 tokens.
requirements.quote: We optimize the shared policy with GRPO using a learning rate of 1 × 10−6 and no explicit KL penalty.

contract.stated_compute: Our implementation is built on verl with an FSDP2 actor and asynchronous vLLM rollout workers. Policy weights are synchronized to the rollout workers after each update to maintain on-policy sampling. Browser execution is parallelized independently from model rollout, with up to 72 concurrent evaluations and a per-example hard timeout of 2,400 seconds.

full.summary: WebLoop addresses functional Web generation by jointly learning Generator, Critic, and Refiner roles within a shared policy, where the Critic is execution-free at inference but receives execution-derived credit during training. The method trains the Critic with requirement-level discriminability labels and downstream refinement helpfulness, then optimizes all three roles with role-specific group-relative GRPO. With Qwen3.5-9B, WebLoop reaches 41.5 Overall on WebRise and 38.9% accuracy on WebGen-Bench, improving the base model by 11.3 and 15.4 points respectively.

tolerance.why: Rule 2: WebRise Overall is an accuracy-like percentage metric on a test set of 442 tasks (fewer than 2,000 examples, so Rule 2 does not apply). Rule 3 applies: it is a bounded score on a smaller set, so the tolerance is 2.0 absolute points. The paper reports no std over repeated runs, so Rule 1 does not apply.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify the exact prompt templates for Generator, Critic, and Refiner; it only says complete role-specific prompts are in Sec. D, which is not included in the provided text.
assumptions.quote: The Critic inspects an imperfect implementation against the task requirements and produces requirement-level judgments and repair guidance.
assumptions.chosen: Reconstruct prompts from the described conditioning contexts and output formats, ensuring the Critic outputs requirement-level judgments and repair guidance and the Generator/Refiner output complete HTML.
options: Reconstruct prompts from the described conditioning contexts and output formats
Use generic instruction prompts without requirement-level structured output
Request the authors' released prompts upon acceptance
assumptions.rationale: The paper states the Critic predicts whether each explicit requirement is satisfied and provides repair guidance, and the Generator/Refiner produce complete HTML implementations; these constraints are sufficient to build faithful prompts even without Sec. D.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify how to parse the Critic's free-form output into requirement-level binary predictions z_hat_j,q for discriminability computation.
assumptions.quote: Critiques that cannot be parsed into the required requirement-level judgments receive the minimum Critic reward and do not instantiate downstream refinement branches.
assumptions.chosen: Use a structured output format enforced by the prompt, and treat unparseable critiques as minimum Critic reward with no downstream refinement branches, as stated in Appendix A.2.
options: Use a structured output format (e.g., JSON or per-requirement labels) enforced by the prompt
Use a separate parser model or heuristic string matching
Treat unparseable critiques as minimum reward and skip downstream refinement
assumptions.rationale: The paper explicitly says critiques that cannot be parsed into required requirement-level judgments receive the minimum Critic reward and do not instantiate downstream refinement branches, so a structured parser is the faithful choice.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify the exact browser automation stack, headless browser version, or timeout handling beyond the per-example hard timeout of 2,400 seconds.
assumptions.quote: Browser execution is parallelized independently from model rollout, with up to 72 concurrent evaluations and a per-example hard timeout of 2,400 seconds.
assumptions.chosen: Use Playwright with Chromium, as it is the most common modern browser automation stack for executable Web evaluation and supports the required interaction and assertion execution.
options: Use Playwright with Chromium
Use Selenium with Chrome
Use Puppeteer with Chromium
assumptions.rationale: The paper only says browser execution is parallelized with up to 72 concurrent evaluations and a 2,400-second timeout; the specific stack is not pinned, so a standard headless Chromium automation library is the conventional choice.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify the exact GRPO clipping parameter εclip, the normalization epsilon εnorm, or the number of optimization epochs per rollout batch.
assumptions.quote: Our implementation is built on verl with an FSDP2 actor and asynchronous vLLM rollout workers.
assumptions.chosen: Use common GRPO defaults: εclip = 0.2, εnorm = 1e-8, and one epoch per rollout batch, following the verl framework defaults.
options: Use common GRPO defaults: εclip = 0.2, εnorm = 1e-8, one epoch per batch
Tune these on a validation set
Use the values from the verl framework defaults
assumptions.rationale: The paper states the implementation is built on verl with FSDP2 actor and asynchronous vLLM rollout workers, so verl's default GRPO hyperparameters are the most faithful convention when the paper omits them.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify how the initial-state contract and Interaction Contract Graph are represented or executed for the 2,880 training tasks, beyond saying they follow WebRISE.
assumptions.quote: Following WebRISE (Meng et al., 2026), each task is associated with an Interaction Contract Graph Gx that specifies browser interactions and functional assertions.
assumptions.chosen: Reuse the WebRISE ICG format and executor directly, since the paper says the construction follows WebRISE and uses the same browser executor for evaluation.
options: Reuse the WebRISE ICG format and executor directly
Reimplement the ICG format from the WebRISE paper
Use a simplified state-transition format
assumptions.rationale: The paper explicitly follows WebRISE for the Interaction Contract Graph and uses the same browser executor for WebRise evaluation, so reusing the WebRISE format is the most faithful and lowest-risk choice.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify the exact task batch size scheduling, gradient accumulation, or whether the 64-task batch is split across GPUs.
assumptions.quote: Training uses 3K text-conditioned Web generation tasks with a task batch size of 64.
assumptions.chosen: Use task batch size 64 with gradient accumulation as needed to fit the available hardware, keeping the effective batch size at 64.
options: Use task batch size 64 with gradient accumulation to fit memory
Use a smaller batch and scale the learning rate
Use the largest batch that fits without accumulation
assumptions.rationale: The paper states a task batch size of 64, so preserving the effective batch size is important for faithful reproduction; gradient accumulation is a standard implementation detail when memory is limited.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify the exact evaluation protocol for WebRise beyond using the same Interaction Contract Graph and browser executor, including how Overall is computed from T, Re, and Ri.
assumptions.quote: WebRise contains 442 tasks and reports transition validity T , explicit requirement coverage Re, implicit requirement coverage Ri, and their average Overall score.
assumptions.chosen: Compute Overall as the average of T, Re, and Ri, following the WebRISE benchmark definition, since the paper says WebRise reports these metrics and their average Overall score.
options: Compute Overall as the average of T, Re, and Ri
Use the WebRISE official Overall definition
Weight T, Re, and Ri differently
assumptions.rationale: The paper explicitly states WebRise reports transition validity T, explicit requirement coverage Re, implicit requirement coverage Ri, and their average Overall score, so the average is the stated definition.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify how to handle tasks where no valid imperfect draft exists beyond saying they contribute only initial-generation samples.
assumptions.quote: If Y− x is empty, no Critic or Refiner branch is expanded for that task.
assumptions.chosen: Skip Critic and Refiner branches for those tasks and include only Generator samples in the batch, as stated in Appendix A.2.
options: Skip Critic and Refiner branches for those tasks and include only Generator samples in the batch
Resample until a valid imperfect draft is found
Use the best valid draft even if it fully solves the task
assumptions.rationale: The paper explicitly says if Y-_x is empty, no Critic or Refiner branch is expanded for that task, so this is the faithful behavior.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify the exact seed or random initialization for the policy, browser evaluation, or data ordering.
assumptions.quote: Unless otherwise stated, controlled comparisons use the same backbone initialization, training-task distribution, browser evaluation infrastructure, and metric computation.
assumptions.chosen: Use a fixed seed for reproducibility and document it, since the paper reports no variance across seeds and controlled comparisons use the same initialization.
options: Use a fixed seed for reproducibility
Use multiple seeds and report variance
Use the default seed of the training framework
assumptions.rationale: The paper says controlled comparisons use the same backbone initialization and training-task distribution, implying a fixed setup; a fixed seed is the standard convention for reproducible RL training.

assumptions.gap: The paper does not specify how the Critic's repair guidance is formatted or how the Refiner consumes it beyond conditioning on the critique.
assumptions.quote: The Critic inspects an imperfect implementation against the task requirements and produces requirement-level judgments and repair guidance.
assumptions.chosen: A combination of requirement-level verdicts and free-form guidance, matching the paper's description that the Critic produces requirement-level judgments and repair guidance.
options: Free-form natural language repair suggestions
Structured per-requirement fix suggestions
A combination of requirement-level verdicts and free-form guidance
assumptions.rationale: The paper states the Critic produces requirement-level judgments and repair guidance, and Fig. 2 shows both diagnosis scores and fix suggestions, so a combined format is faithful.

match_target.why: C1 is the paper's headline central result on the primary benchmark (WebRise Overall with Qwen3.5-9B), and it is the cheapest target because the 9B model is the smallest backbone used for all controlled experiments and the WebRise Text-modality evaluation is the main reported setting. Reproducing C1 requires the full WebLoop training loop but avoids the larger 27B compute of C5/C6 and the multi-modality evaluation of C7.

full.stated_compute: Our implementation is built on verl with an FSDP2 actor and asynchronous vLLM rollout workers. Policy weights are synchronized to the rollout workers after each update to maintain on-policy sampling. Browser execution is parallelized independently from model rollout, with up to 72 concurrent evaluations and a per-example hard timeout of 2,400 seconds.

routeInfo.why: The paper links a repository (https://github.com/IIGROUP/WebLoop), but the claim contract's data section states the WebLoop training corpus (2,880 tasks) and its construction assets 'will be publicly released upon acceptance' — i.e., not yet available. The two evaluation benchmarks (WebRise, WebGen-Bench) are public, but the central claim C1 requires the trained WebLoop checkpoint, which depends on the unreleased 2,880-task corpus with Interaction Contract Graphs, plus the authors' role-specific prompts (Sec. D, not included) and the exact ICG executor. Even if the repo exists, the training data and prompts are missing, so the released code cannot reproduce C1 as-is. Additionally, the stated compute (8-16 GPUs for several days of GRPO training with 12 browser-evaluated candidates per rollout) is far beyond this machine's ~60-minute budget, and the backbone (Qwen3.5-9B) plus verl/FSDP2/vLLM stack is not runnable here. This is a reimplement-from-paper situation, and even then only a heavily scaled-down proxy is feasible.

feasibility.scale_down_plan: If forced to produce a number within budget: (1) substitute a small open instruct model (e.g., a 1-3B model) for Qwen3.5-9B; (2) use a tiny subset of WebRise (e.g., 20-40 tasks) or a synthetic set of ~50 hand-built HTML tasks with simple ICG-style assertions; (3) run only 1-2 GRPO updates with ng=2, nc=1, nr=1 (instead of 3/3/3) and no browser-in-the-loop (use a lightweight DOM/JS assertion runner instead of full Chromium); (4) evaluate only the Generator and a single Refine pass. Expected effect: the resulting Overall will be far below 41.5 (likely in the 10-25 range depending on backbone and task difficulty) and cannot be compared to the paper's number; it can only demonstrate that the loop mechanism (Gen -> Critic -> Refine with execution-derived credit) is implementable and directionally improves over a base model on the tiny subset. This would be a mechanism demonstration, not a reproduction of C1.
feasibility.est_runtime_on_this_machine: Full C1 reproduction (train Qwen3.5-9B WebLoop on 2,880 tasks with browser-in-the-loop GRPO, then evaluate on 442 WebRise tasks) is not feasible on this machine: the paper reports 8-16 GPUs for several days. Even a single evaluation pass of the trained model over 442 tasks with browser execution would take many hours. A scaled-down proxy (small open backbone, tiny task subset, few GRPO steps, no full browser harness) could run in ~30-60 min but would not reproduce the 41.5 number.

files.purpose: Single source of truth for all hyperparameters (backbone, ng/nc/nr, GRPO lr, clip, lambda, critic schedule, reward weights, seeds, task counts, timeouts).

Build a tiny synthetic WebRise-style task suite: each task has a natural-language description, explicit requirements, implicit requirements, and an Interaction Contract Graph (list of browser interactions + DOM/JS assertions) executed by a lightweight headless runner. Also provides the held-out eval split.

Lightweight execution environment: renders candidate HTML in a headless DOM (Playwright/Chromium if available, else a jsdom-style fallback via a minimal Python HTML+regex assertion runner) and returns E(y; Gx) = (T, Re, Ri, z) per the ICG. Enforces per-example timeout.

Reconstructed role-specific prompts (assumption A1): Generator (task -> complete HTML), Critic (task + source only, no execution info -> structured per-requirement verdicts + repair guidance, assumption A2/A10), Refiner (task + current HTML + critique -> complete revised HTML).
Parse the Critic's structured output into per-requirement binary predictions z_hat_j,q; unparseable critiques get minimum Critic reward and instantiate no refinement branches (assumption A2).

Per-task rollout: sample ng=3 initial generations, execute each, select median-reward valid-but-imperfect draft yb (skip Critic/Refiner if none, assumption A8), sample nc=3 critiques, sample nr=3 refinements per critique; return all samples with rewards and role tags.

Compute Critic credit: discriminability D(cj) = a_fail + a_pass - 1 with single-class rescaling to [-1,1] (R8), helpfulness H(cj) = mean refinement reward - base reward (R9), and staged schedule D-only for m<=15 then H + 0.2D (R10).

Role-specific group-relative advantage A_o = (r(o) - mu_g) / (sigma_g + eps_norm) (R12), merged optimization batch across roles (R13), clipped GRPO loss with lr=1e-6, no KL penalty, eps_clip=0.2, eps_norm=1e-8 (R15, A4).

Training loop: for each of a small number of updates, run rollouts over the tiny train set, compute critic credit and role-specific advantages, take one GRPO step on the shared policy. Logs per-update stats.
Evaluate base model, WebLoop (Gen) first-pass, and WebLoop (Refine) after one complete loop on the held-out tiny task set; compute T, Re, Ri and Overall = mean(T, Re, Ri) (assumption A7).

Entrypoint: sets seed, builds tasks, runs smoke test, trains, evaluates, writes results/metrics.json with the three Overall numbers plus a clear 'mechanism_demonstration_not_C1' flag and the paper's target 41.5 for reference.

steps: Create project dirs: results/, cache/, and write config.py with all hyperparameters above.

Implement tasks.py: hand-author ~20 tiny HTML tasks (e.g., 'button toggles a div', 'form validates email', 'counter increments on click') each with description, explicit requirements, implicit requirements, and an ICG of interactions + assertions.

Implement executor.py: try to import playwright and launch headless Chromium; if unavailable, fall back to a pure-Python HTML/JS-lite assertion runner that checks DOM structure and simple event handlers via regex/BeautifulSoup. Return (T, Re, Ri, z) and enforce per-example timeout.

Implement prompts.py with the three reconstructed role prompts (A1): Generator emits complete HTML; Critic sees only task + source and must emit a JSON list of {requirement_id, verdict, guidance}; Refiner sees task + current HTML + critique and emits complete revised HTML.
Implement critic_parser.py: parse the Critic JSON; on failure return min reward and mark no-refinement (A2).

Implement rollout.py: for each task, sample ng=3 Generations, execute, pick median-reward valid-but-imperfect draft yb (skip Critic/Refiner if none, A8), sample nc=3 Critiques, sample nr=3 Refinements per critique; tag each sample with role and reward.
Implement credit.py: compute D(cj) with single-class rescaling (R8), H(cj) (R9), and staged critic reward D-only for m<=15 else H+0.2D (R10).
Implement grpo.py: role-specific group-relative advantage (R12), merge roles into one batch (R13), clipped GRPO loss with lr=1e-6, no KL, eps_clip=0.2, eps_norm=1e-8 (R15, A4).
Implement train.py: loop num_updates times over the tiny train set, run rollouts, compute credit and advantages, take one optimizer step, log mean reward per role.
Implement evaluate.py: run base model, WebLoop (Gen) first-pass, and WebLoop (Refine) after one loop on the held-out eval tasks; compute T, Re, Ri and Overall = mean(T, Re, Ri).

Implement reproduce.py: set seed, build tasks, run smoke test (2 tasks, ng=1, nc=1, nr=1, 1 update), then full scaled run, then write results/metrics.json with base/Gen/Refine Overall, the paper target 41.5, and a 'mechanism_demonstration_not_C1' flag.
Run reproduce.py end-to-end and inspect results/metrics.json.

config.num_updates: 4 (scaled down; critic schedule threshold kept at 15 so all updates are D-only, matching R10's first phase)
config.browser_stack: Playwright+Chromium if importable, else built-in regex/DOM fallback (assumption A3)

plan.approach: The route is paper_only: the WebLoop training corpus (2,880 tasks with ICGs), the trained Qwen3.5-9B checkpoints, the role-specific prompts (Sec. D), and the WebRise ICG executor are all unavailable, and the stated compute (8-16 GPUs for days) is far beyond this machine. I therefore build a faithful, heavily scaled-down mechanism demonstration of the Generator-Critic-Refiner loop with execution-derived credit: a tiny synthetic suite of HTML tasks with ICG-style DOM/JS assertions, a small open instruct backbone (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct or similar), and a few GRPO updates using the paper's role-specific group-relative advantage, the r_web = 0.50T + 0.25Re + 0.25Ri reward, the D/H critic credit schedule (D-only for the first 15 updates, then H + 0.2D), and the ng/nc/nr branching structure. Evaluation runs the same assertion runner on a held-out tiny task set and reports Overall = mean(T, Re, Ri) for base vs. WebLoop (Gen) vs. WebLoop (Refine). The result will be far below 41.5 and is explicitly a mechanism demonstration, not a reproduction of C1; metrics.json records this caveat alongside the numbers.
plan.smoke_test: python reproduce.py --smoke: uses 2 train tasks and 2 eval tasks, ng=1, nc=1, nr=1, 1 GRPO update, max_new_tokens=128. Verifies that (a) the executor returns (T, Re, Ri, z) for a hand-written correct and a hand-written broken HTML, (b) the Critic parser yields per-requirement verdicts, (c) one GRPO step runs without NaN, and (d) metrics.json is written with three Overall values.
plan.budget_plan: Setup (env check, pip install playwright/beautifulsoup4 if needed, write config/tasks/executor/prompts/parser): ~15 min. Smoke test (2 tasks, 1 update): ~5 min. Full scaled run (12 train tasks, 4 updates, ng=3/nc=3/nr=3, 8 eval tasks, three evaluation passes): ~30 min. Buffer for debugging and metrics writing: ~10 min. Total ~60 min. If Playwright/Chromium cannot be installed, the pure-Python fallback runner keeps the run within budget at the cost of lower execution fidelity.
intermediate_checks: Executor sanity: a hand-written fully-correct HTML scores T=Re=Ri=1.0; a hand-written broken HTML scores near 0; a partially-correct HTML scores in between.
Task suite: confirm >=12 train and >=8 eval tasks, each with >=2 explicit and >=1 implicit requirement, and that every ICG assertion is executable by the chosen runner.
Critic parser: feed 5 hand-written critiques (valid JSON, malformed, missing fields) and confirm correct parsing or min-reward fallback.
Parameter count: print trainable parameter count of the backbone and confirm it matches the chosen small model (not 9B).
Baseline sanity: base model Overall on eval tasks should be low but non-zero (e.g., 0.05-0.30); if exactly 0, the executor or prompt is broken.
Reward range: confirm all r_web values lie in [0,1] and that the median-reward draft selection picks a valid-but-imperfect candidate when one exists.
GRPO advantage: confirm group-relative advantages have mean ~0 within each role group and finite values.
Timing: measure per-task rollout wall time and extrapolate to confirm the full scaled run fits the budget.

contract.summary: Anomaly detection methods struggle with data exhibiting varying local densities, where distance-based methods miss local anomalies and density-based methods require careful parameter selection and incur quadratic time complexity. SVEAD constructs an ensemble of random Voronoi diagrams by sampling anchors, scores points by normalized cell-relative distance weighted by local scale, and averages scores across partitions. Across 45 ADBench datasets it achieves the highest average AUC-ROC (0.8538) and AUC-PR (0.5000) among 12 baselines, including 0.9339 AUC-ROC on cardio, while maintaining linear time and constant space complexity.
